Practitioners use causal pathways to show how one change leads to another, helping to explain why an intervention is expected to produce a specific result. This concept matters in development work, particularly in impact evaluations and policy planning. However, causal pathways can be contested when there are multiple plausible sequences of events.
sources: OECD DAC and Sida, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results Based Management, entry 'Results chain' (2014). https://cdn.sida.se/publications/files/sida37877en-glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management.pdf
National Health Mission, Janani Suraksha Yojana (2026). https://nhm.gov.in/index1.php?lang=1&level=3&sublinkid=841&lid=309
causal-pathway.example: The intended causal pathway of Janani Suraksha Yojana runs from cash assistance to poor pregnant women, to more births in health facilities, to skilled care at delivery, and from there to lower maternal and neonatal mortality. Each link is an assumption that an evaluation can test.

computer-vision.definition: Computer Vision is a field of Artificial Intelligence (AI) that enables computers to "see" and interpret information from images and videos. For development practitioners, it offers powerful tools to analyze large datasets quickly, often where manual observation is impractical. This includes monitoring changes in land use for urban planning, assessing crop health from drone imagery to inform agricultural interventions, or identifying informal settlements from satellite photos to better target public services like PDS. It's increasingly used to digitize and extract data from physical documents, speeding up administrative processes. While powerful, its application requires careful consideration of data privacy and potential Algorithmic Bias, especially when used for surveillance or resource allocation.
sources: Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y. and Courville, A., Deep Learning, Chapter 12.2: Computer Vision, MIT Press (2016). https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/applications.html
computer-vision.example: A research team trains a model to read handwritten entries in scanned registers, then has staff check a sample of the digitised records against the originals before using them.

data-tables.definition: Data tables are structured displays of data in rows and columns, providing underlying information in a format that can be easily read and analyzed. Practitioners use data tables when they need to present complex data in a clear and accessible way, especially when visualizations like charts may not be sufficient or accessible to all users, such as those with visual impairments.
sources: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, Tables Tutorial (2026). https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/tables/
data-tables.example: An online report places a data table beneath each chart, with column and row headers marked up so that a screen reader announces the header for each cell as the user moves through the table.

extractive-institutions.definition: Extractive institutions are political and economic arrangements that benefit a small elite at the expense of the wider population. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson use the term for systems in which political rights are limited and economic rules let the elite extract resources from everyone else. Their work argues that such institutions tend to persist, because those who gain from them have little reason to give up power, and that they are associated with lower long-run prosperity. The term is used in contrast to inclusive institutions.
sources: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2024 (2024). https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2024/popular-information/

Banerjee, A. and Iyer, L., History, Institutions, and Economic Performance: The Legacy of Colonial Land Tenure Systems in India, American Economic Review 95(4) (2005). https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/0002828054825574
extractive-institutions.example: Banerjee and Iyer (2005) found that districts of British India where land revenue rights were given to landlords had lower agricultural investment and productivity after independence than districts where cultivators held those rights. Their study is often cited as evidence that institutions set up in the colonial period can shape outcomes long after it ends.

fairness.definition: In AI, fairness covers concerns for equality and equity, including how a system deals with harmful bias and discrimination. NIST notes that standards of fairness are hard to define, because perceptions of fairness differ across cultures and can change with the application. Several mathematical fairness measures exist, and some of them cannot all be satisfied at once. A practitioner uses the term when checking whether an AI system used in a programme, for example to screen applicants or target benefits, treats different groups equitably. Reducing measured bias does not by itself make a system fair.
sources: NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1, section 3.7 (2023). https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf
NIST, The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms, entry 'fairness metric' (2023). https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/
fairness.example: Before using a model to rank households for a welfare scheme, a team checks whether its error rates differ between groups, such as women-headed and men-headed households, and whether people without smartphones are left out of the data altogether.

fcdo-logframe.definition: The FCDO logframe is the logical framework format used in programmes funded by the UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office. Like other logframes, it sets out a programme's results chain, from inputs and activities through outputs and outcomes to impact, with indicators, sources of data and the assumptions that link each level. FCDO's Programme Operating Framework requires every programme to be reviewed at least once a year against an agreed results framework or logframe, so organisations receiving FCDO money usually report against one. The format is often criticised for assuming a linear path from activities to results, which can sit uneasily with programmes that need to adapt as they go.
sources: UK Government, FCDO Programme Operating Framework: overview, rule 19 (2025). https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/fcdo-programme-operating-framework/fcdo-programme-operating-framework-overview

OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, 2nd ed., entry 'Logical framework' (2023), trilingual edition published with IsDB (2024). https://www.isdb.org/sites/default/files/media/documents/2024-04/OECD%20Glossary%20of%20Key%20Evaluation%20Terms%20in%20Arabic%20English%20French.pdf
fcdo-logframe.example: An NGO bidding for FCDO funding for a climate resilience project in Bangladesh sets out its intended outcome, the indicators that will show progress towards it, and the assumptions behind each step in a logframe, then reports against that logframe in each annual review.

feature-engineering.definition: Feature engineering is the work of adjusting and reworking the predictors (features) given to a model so that it can better pick up the relationship between predictors and the outcome. It includes transforming a single variable, combining variables into products or ratios, and re-expressing a variable in a more useful form. It usually depends on knowledge of the subject and on trying many alternative representations, because the best one is rarely known in advance.
sources: Kuhn, M. and Johnson, K., Feature Engineering and Selection: A Practical Approach for Predictive Models, Preface (2019). https://bookdown.org/max/FES/
feature-engineering.example: A team predicting school dropout combines a child's age and grade into a single 'over-age for grade' variable, and turns a household's list of assets into a count, because these new features predict dropout better than the raw columns.

finance-commission.definition: The Finance Commission is a body that Article 280 of the Constitution of India requires the President to constitute every fifth year or earlier. It recommends how the net proceeds of shareable Union taxes are divided between the Union and the states (vertical devolution) and how the states' share is divided among them (horizontal devolution), as well as grants-in-aid to states and other matters referred to it. Its recommendations shape how much untied money each state has for its own priorities, which matters to anyone working on state budgets or the funding of schemes.
sources: Sixteenth Finance Commission of India, About Us (2026). https://fincomindia.nic.in/
Ministry of Finance, Explanatory Memorandum as to the Action Taken on the Recommendations Made by the Sixteenth Finance Commission (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/16fc.pdf
finance-commission.example: The Fifteenth Finance Commission set the states' share at 41 per cent of the divisible pool. The Sixteenth Finance Commission, whose report covers 2026-27 to 2030-31, recommended retaining it at 41 per cent, and the Union government accepted this.

financial-inclusion.definition: Financial inclusion means that individuals and businesses have access to useful and affordable financial products and services, such as transactions, payments, savings, credit and insurance, delivered in a responsible and sustainable way. In India, the RBI's National Strategy for Financial Inclusion cites the Rangarajan Committee's definition, the process of ensuring access to financial services, and timely and adequate credit where needed, for vulnerable groups such as weaker sections and low-income groups at an affordable cost. Practitioners use the term when discussing how to extend these services to people who are poorly served by formal finance.
sources: Reserve Bank of India, National Strategy for Financial Inclusion 2019-2024 (2020). https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/PublicationReportDetails.aspx?ID=1154
Press Information Bureau, 67 and Rising: India's Financial Inclusion Gains Momentum (6 August 2025). https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2025/aug/doc202586601201.pdf
financial-inclusion.example: The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana opens basic bank accounts for people who did not have one. A PIB note of August 2025 reported 55.98 crore beneficiaries under the scheme.

first-appellate-authority.definition: The First Appellate Authority is the officer, senior in rank to the Public Information Officer, to whom a first appeal lies under section 19(1) of India's Right to Information Act, 2005, within the same public authority. A person who gets no decision within the time the Act allows, or who is aggrieved by the PIO's decision, may appeal within thirty days, and the officer may admit a later appeal if there was sufficient cause for the delay. The appeal must normally be decided within thirty days, extendable to forty-five. A second appeal then lies with the Central or State Information Commission within ninety days.
sources: Government of India, The Right to Information Act, 2005, section 19 (as published by the Central Information Commission). https://cic.gov.in/sites/default/files/RTI-Act_English.pdf
first-appellate-authority.example: A resident who asks a block office for ration distribution records and gets no reply within thirty days files a first appeal with the officer the office has named as its First Appellate Authority, who must be senior to the PIO who failed to respond.

fiscal-deficit.definition: The fiscal deficit is the difference between a government's total expenditure and its total receipts, excluding debt capital receipts (borrowing). It therefore shows the government's total borrowing requirement for the year. Practitioners use it to judge the state of public finances and the room a government has to fund programmes.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Budget at a Glance 2026-27 (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/Budget_at_Glance/budget_at_a_glance.pdf
Ministry of Finance, Budget Speech 2021-22, paragraphs 141 and 144 (2021). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/budget2021-22/doc/Budget_Speech.pdf
fiscal-deficit.example: The Union Budget of February 2021 put the fiscal deficit for 2020-21 at 9.5 per cent of GDP in the revised estimates, and the government laid a statement of deviation from the FRBM Act's targets because of the pandemic.

fiscal-federalism.definition: Fiscal federalism examines how financial powers (raising revenue, spending and borrowing) are shared and distributed across different levels of government, like the Union, state, and local bodies in India. For practitioners, understanding this concept matters when designing or advocating for development programs, as it explains how resources flow and where funding decisions are made. It highlights the 'vertical imbalance' where states often spend more than they can raise, and 'horizontal imbalance' between richer and poorer states. Debates often arise over the conditions attached to central grants or the fairness of resource devolution, directly impacting the autonomy and capacity of state and local governments to deliver services like health or education.
sources: Oates, W. E., An Essay on Fiscal Federalism, Journal of Economic Literature 37(3) (1999). https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jel.37.3.1120
Ministry of Finance, Explanatory Memorandum as to the Action Taken on the Recommendations Made by the Sixteenth Finance Commission (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/16fc.pdf
fiscal-federalism.example: India's Finance Commission recommends how the net proceeds of Union taxes are shared between the Union and the states and among the states, and what grants states should receive. Centrally Sponsored Schemes, in which the Union funds part of a scheme that states run, are another channel of transfers.

flailing-state.definition: A flailing state, in Lant Pritchett's term, is a state whose capable head is no longer reliably connected to the arms and legs of implementation. Its central institutions can design good policy, but its field agents routinely do not carry out the tasks assigned to them, so practice diverges widely from the rules on paper. Pritchett applied the term to India in 2009, drawing on examples from health, education and routine services such as issuing driving licences.
sources: Pritchett, L., Is India a Flailing State?: Detours on the Four Lane Highway to Modernization, HKS Faculty Research Working Paper RWP09-013 (2009). https://www.hks.harvard.edu/publications/india-flailing-state-detours-four-lane-highway-modernization
flailing-state.example: A state health department issues sound protocols for primary health centres, but staff absence and unrecorded fees in the centres themselves mean patients receive something quite different from what the protocols promise.

focus-group-discussion.definition: A focus group discussion (FGD) is a qualitative data collection method in which a trained facilitator leads a discussion among a small group of people, usually 6 to 12, who share characteristics relevant to the topic. Practitioners use FGDs to understand the range of views, norms and experiences in a community, for example barriers to using a health scheme or reasons for not adopting a farming practice. Because participants respond to each other, FGDs can bring out attitudes that individual interviews miss. They show the range of opinions in a group and not how common each opinion is, so the findings cannot be generalised to a whole population. Skilled facilitation is needed so that a few people do not dominate.
sources: Catholic Relief Services, Practical Guide: Focus Group Discussions (2022). https://www.crs.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/2022_08_practical_guide_fgds_final_high_res_eng.pdf
focus-group-discussion.example: Before revising a family planning communication campaign, an NGO holds separate FGDs with young married women and with their mothers-in-law to understand what each group has heard about a new method and who decides whether it is used.

foreign-direct-investment.definition: Foreign direct investment (FDI) is cross-border investment made by a resident of one economy with the aim of establishing a lasting interest in an enterprise resident in another economy. Under the OECD and IMF standards, a lasting interest is shown when the investor owns at least 10 per cent of the voting power of the enterprise. FDI can take the form of setting up new operations or buying into existing firms. Practitioners look at FDI when analysing growth, jobs and technology transfer, and also its effects on local competition and the environment.
sources: Statistics Canada, Foreign Direct Investment, quoting the OECD Benchmark Definition of Foreign Direct Investment, 4th ed. (2016). https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/13-607-x/2016001/48-eng.htm
foreign-direct-investment.example: A foreign electronics company that builds and owns a factory in India making phones for the Indian market is making a foreign direct investment. A foreign fund that buys a 2 per cent stake in a listed Indian company is making a portfolio investment.

forest-rights-act.definition: The Forest Rights Act (FRA), formally the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, recognises and vests forest rights in forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers. Section 3(1) lists these rights, which secure individual or community tenure or both. They include the right to live on and cultivate forest land, rights over minor forest produce, grazing and other community uses, habitat rights for primitive tribal groups, and the right to protect, regenerate and manage community forest resources. Rights are recognised only for land occupied before 13 December 2005, are heritable but cannot be sold or transferred, and are registered jointly in the names of both spouses. Practitioners engage with the FRA in work on land tenure, community resource management and the rights of forest-dwelling communities.
sources: Government of India, The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (No. 2 of 2007), as published by PRS Legislative Research. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_parliament/2006/the-scheduled-tribes-and-other-traditional-forest-dwellers-recognition-of-forest-rights-act-2006.pdf
forest-rights-act.example: An NGO in Odisha supports a Gram Sabha to prepare a claim for community forest resource rights under section 3(1)(i), mapping the forest the village has traditionally protected so that it can manage that forest under the Act.

formative-evaluation.definition: Formative evaluation is evaluation intended to improve performance or to inform the planning of a later phase, often carried out while an intervention is being implemented. It can also be done for other reasons, such as compliance or as part of a larger evaluation. Practitioners use it to adjust an intervention while it is running, by gathering feedback from participants, testing materials and changing what does not work.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, 2nd ed., entry 'Formative evaluation' (2023), trilingual edition published with IsDB (2024). https://www.isdb.org/sites/default/files/media/documents/2024-04/OECD%20Glossary%20of%20Key%20Evaluation%20Terms%20in%20Arabic%20English%20French.pdf
formative-evaluation.example: Six months into a maternal health programme, a team interviews health workers and mothers to find out why few women are claiming a cash incentive, and uses the findings to change how the scheme is publicised before it expands to new districts.

frbm-act.definition: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 sets out the Union government's responsibility for fiscal discipline and long-term macroeconomic stability. The Act and its rules came into force on 5 July 2004. In its current form it requires the Union government to limit the fiscal deficit to 3 per cent of GDP, and to endeavour to bring general government debt to 60 per cent and Union government debt to 40 per cent of GDP. The government must lay fiscal policy statements before Parliament with each budget, and must explain any deviation from the targets. Practitioners use the Act to judge the government's fiscal room and the pressure on budgets for social sector schemes. The targets have repeatedly been missed or deferred.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Statements of Fiscal Policy as required under the FRBM Act, 2003, Preface (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/frbm1.pdf
Ministry of Finance, Budget Speech 2020-21, paragraph on FRBM deviation (2020). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/budget2020-21/doc/Budget_Speech.pdf
Ministry of Finance, Budget Speech 2021-22, paragraph 144 (2021). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/budget2021-22/doc/Budget_Speech.pdf
frbm-act.example: In the Budget of February 2020, before the pandemic, the Finance Minister took a deviation of 0.5 per cent of GDP from the fiscal deficit path for 2019-20 and 2020-21, citing the Act's provision for structural reforms with unanticipated fiscal effects. In February 2021 a further statement of deviation was laid because of the pandemic.

functionings.definition: In Amartya Sen's capability approach, functionings are the 'beings and doings' a person has actually achieved, such as being well nourished, being educated, getting married or travelling. Capabilities are the real opportunities a person has to achieve such functionings, so functionings can be thought of as capabilities that have been realised. Practitioners use the term when they assess what people are actually able to be and do as a result of a programme, beyond the income or goods they receive.
sources: Robeyns, I. and Byskov, M. F., The Capability Approach, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, section 2.1. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/capability-approach/
functionings.example: Two women each receive the same food ration. One is well nourished and the other is not, because she is ill and cannot absorb the food. The ration is the same, but their functioning of being well nourished differs.

gender-budgeting.definition: Gender budgeting means integrating a clear gender perspective into the whole budget process, using special processes and analytical tools to promote policies and spending that help achieve gender equality goals. Practitioners use it to analyse how budgets affect women and men differently, to argue for different allocations and to monitor government commitments. India's Union budget carries a Gender Budget Statement (Statement 13) in three parts. Part A lists schemes with 100 per cent of the provision for women and girls, Part B schemes with 30 to 99 per cent, and Part C schemes with less than 30 per cent. How schemes are classified is open to debate, because a scheme listed in full can serve whole households.
sources: OECD, 2022 OECD Survey on Gender Budgeting: Glossary of key terms (2022). https://webfs.oecd.org/governmentataglance/Budgeting/2022%20OECD%20Survey%20on%20Gender%20Budgeting_Glossary.pdf
Ministry of Finance, Expenditure Profile 2026-27, Statement 13: Gender Budget (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/eb/stat13.pdf
gender-budgeting.example: In the 2026-27 Gender Budget Statement, the entire allocations for PMAY-Gramin and PMAY-Urban housing appear in Part A as 100 per cent for women, while Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0 appear in Part B. Readers who want to know how much actually reaches women need to look at how each scheme is classified.

gestalt-principles.definition: Gestalt principles describe how people perceive visual elements as organised groups and wholes. Max Wertheimer's 1923 paper set out factors such as proximity (elements close together are seen as a group), similarity (like elements band together), closure and good continuation, and later work added others. Practitioners use these principles in data visualisation to make the intended groupings in a chart easy to see, for example by placing related bars together or giving one series a single colour.
sources: Wertheimer, M., Laws of Organization in Perceptual Forms (1923; English translation 1938), Classics in the History of Psychology, York University. https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Wertheimer/Forms/forms.htm
gestalt-principles.example: In a chart comparing districts, a designer places the bars for each state next to each other and gives every district of one state the same colour, so readers see the states as groups without reading a legend.

ggplot2.definition: ggplot2 is an R package for creating graphics declaratively, based on the Grammar of Graphics. The user supplies the data, says how variables map to aesthetics such as position or colour, and chooses the geometric objects to draw, and the package handles the details. A plot is built up from layers, scales, facets and a coordinate system, which makes it easy to change one part of a chart without rebuilding the rest. M&E and research teams use it to produce consistent, publication-quality charts for reports and briefs. Good design still depends on the choices the user makes.
sources: CRAN, ggplot2: Create Elegant Data Visualisations Using the Grammar of Graphics, package page. https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggplot2
Wickham, H., A Layered Grammar of Graphics, Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 19(1) (2010). https://vita.had.co.nz/papers/layered-grammar.pdf
ggplot2.example: An M&E team uses ggplot2 to draw a box plot of home visits per health worker for each district, then adds a facet for each state so that differences between and within states are visible in one figure.

global-value-chains.definition: A global value chain (GVC) breaks up the production of a good or service across countries, with firms specialising in particular tasks and none producing the whole product. Raw materials, parts, semi-finished goods and services may each cross borders before the final product reaches the consumer. The World Bank's World Development Report 2020 finds that GVCs have contributed to growth, jobs and lower poverty in developing countries, and also to inequality and environmental damage. Practitioners use the concept to understand how a local industry fits into international production and what that means for jobs, wages and industrial policy.
sources: World Bank, World Development Report 2020: Trading for Development in the Age of Global Value Chains, Overview (2020). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/32437
global-value-chains.example: A garment factory in Bangladesh may sew clothes designed by a buyer in Europe from fabric made in another Asian country, for sale in shops in North America. The factory is one stage in a chain that crosses several borders.

good-governance.definition: Good governance refers to the exercise of public authority through institutions and processes that are transparent, responsible, accountable, participatory and responsive to the needs of the people. The UN Human Rights Council recognises such government as the foundation on which good governance rests, and links it to the rule of law, a professional public service and action against corruption. Practitioners use the term when assessing how well public institutions deliver services and answer to citizens.
sources: UN Human Rights Council, Resolution 57/5: The role of good governance in the promotion and protection of human rights, A/HRC/RES/57/5 (2024). https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/g24/190/12/pdf/g2419012.pdf
good-governance.example: A district administration that publishes its works lists online, holds open meetings where residents can question officials, and responds to complaints within a fixed time is putting several features of good governance into practice.

government-failure.definition: Government failure describes cases where government action fails to improve outcomes, or makes them worse, when a better outcome was available. In much of the literature it means a government's failure to correct a classic market failure. Keech and Munger propose a broader test, under which government fails whenever an available improvement that would make some people better off and nobody worse off is not chosen or not implemented. Mechanisms include corruption, agency problems, rent-seeking and flawed collective decision-making.
sources: Keech, W. R. and Munger, M. C., The anatomy of government failure, Public Choice 164 (2015). https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/1074129
government-failure.example: A licensing regime meant to steer investment into priority sectors ends up rewarding firms that are good at lobbying officials for licences, so resources go into rent-seeking and the intended improvement in investment does not happen.

gram-sabha.definition: Under Article 243(b) of the Constitution of India, a Gram Sabha is a body consisting of all persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to a village within the area of a village-level Panchayat. Under Article 243A it exercises the powers and functions that the state legislature provides by law. Other laws give it further roles. The Forest Rights Act, 2006, for example, defines the Gram Sabha as an assembly of all adult members of a village with full participation of women, and gives it a central part in recognising forest rights. Practitioners use the term in work on local self-government, community decision-making and natural resource management.
sources: Constitution of India, Articles 243 and 243A, Centre for Law and Policy Research. https://www.constitutionofindia.net/articles/article-243-definitions/

Government of India, The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, section 2(g), as published by PRS Legislative Research. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_parliament/2006/the-scheduled-tribes-and-other-traditional-forest-dwellers-recognition-of-forest-rights-act-2006.pdf
gram-sabha.example: Under the Forest Rights Act, the Gram Sabha starts the process of recognising forest rights by receiving claims from individuals and the community and passing a resolution on them.

grammar-of-graphics.definition: The grammar of graphics is a way of describing any statistical graphic by its components, introduced by Leland Wilkinson and extended by Hadley Wickham's layered grammar. In the layered version a plot is made of data and aesthetic mappings, one or more layers (each with a geometric object, a statistical transformation and a position adjustment), scales, a coordinate system and facets. Because the components are independent, one can be changed without changing the rest. Practitioners meet it through tools such as ggplot2, and it helps them think about a chart as a set of decisions and not as a fixed chart type.
sources: Wickham, H., A Layered Grammar of Graphics, Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 19(1) (2010). https://vita.had.co.nz/papers/layered-grammar.pdf
grammar-of-graphics.example: A scatter plot of district literacy against income and the same data drawn as a binned heat map share their data and mappings. Only the geometric object and statistical transformation differ.

gross-domestic-product.definition: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the monetary value of final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period, such as a quarter or a year. It includes goods and services produced for sale and some non-market production, such as government education services, but excludes unpaid household work. Practitioners use GDP to assess a country's economic performance. It is not a measure of well-being, and it captures poorly environmental damage, the depletion of natural resources and how income is distributed.
sources: Callen, T., Gross Domestic Product: An Economy's All, IMF Finance and Development, Back to Basics (2019). https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/fandd/issues/Series/Back-to-Basics/gross-domestic-product-GDP
Ministry of Finance, Statements of Fiscal Policy as required under the FRBM Act, 2003, Macro-Economic Framework Statement (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/frbm1.pdf
gross-domestic-product.example: India's National Statistics Office estimated real GDP growth for 2025-26 at 7.4 per cent in its first advance estimates.

ground-truth.definition: Ground truth is information obtained by direct observation, as opposed to information produced by inference. In machine learning it is the verified data used to train a model or to check its predictions. Practitioners use ground truth when building or validating predictive models, for example of poverty or crop yields, because a model can be no more accurate than the observations it is checked against.
sources: NIST, The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms, entry 'ground truth' (2023). https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/
ground-truth.example: To validate a model that estimates village poverty from satellite images, a team compares its predictions with consumption measured in a household survey in a sample of the same villages. The survey is the ground truth.

gst-council.definition: The GST Council is a constitutional body set up under Article 279A, inserted by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016. It is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and includes the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance and the Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation, or another minister, nominated by each state. It recommends to the Union and the states which taxes GST subsumes, which goods and services are taxed or exempt, rates, thresholds and other matters. Practitioners working on public finance or on the cost of goods to households follow its decisions.
sources: Constitution of India, Article 279A, Centre for Law and Policy Research. https://www.constitutionofindia.net/articles/article-279a-goods-and-services-tax-council/

Press Information Bureau, GST Council recommends GST rates reduction on several goods (21 July 2018), hosted by the GST Council. https://gstcouncil.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-10/28th_gst_press_information_bureau.pdf
gst-council.example: At its 28th meeting on 21 July 2018, the GST Council recommended reducing the GST rate on sanitary napkins to nil.

habitat-rights.definition: Habitat rights are the rights recognised under section 3(1)(e) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006, namely community tenures of habitat and habitation for primitive tribal groups (now called Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups) and pre-agricultural communities. The Act defines habitat to include the customary habitat and other habitats of these groups in reserved and protected forests. Practitioners use the term when supporting such communities to secure recognition of the wider territory on which their way of life depends.
sources: Government of India, The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, sections 2(h) and 3(1)(e), as published by PRS Legislative Research. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_parliament/2006/the-scheduled-tribes-and-other-traditional-forest-dwellers-recognition-of-forest-rights-act-2006.pdf
habitat-rights.example: A PVTG community works with its Gram Sabha and a support organisation to map the forest area it customarily uses for living, gathering and ritual, and files a habitat rights claim covering that area under section 3(1)(e).

headcount-ratio.definition: The headcount ratio is the share of a population living below a poverty line. Practitioners use it as a simple measure of how widespread poverty is and to track progress against poverty goals. It does not show how far below the line poor people are, so it is often reported alongside poverty gap measures.
sources: World Bank, World Development Indicators, Poverty headcount ratio at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), indicator SI.POV.DDAY, India series. https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/IND/indicator/SI.POV.DDAY?format=json&per_page=60
headcount-ratio.example: World Bank data put India's poverty headcount ratio at the $3.00 a day international line (2021 PPP) at 47.5 per cent in 1993 and 5.3 per cent in 2022.

heterogeneity.definition: Heterogeneity, or heterogeneous treatment effects, means that a programme's effect differs across groups of participants. An average effect for the whole group can hide these differences. Practitioners plan for it when designing evaluations, for example by stratifying the sample so that there are enough members of each subgroup of interest to estimate their effects, and use the results to decide who benefits most.
sources: Gertler, P. J. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, 2nd ed., World Bank and IDB, chapter 9 'Heterogeneous Treatment Effects' (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
heterogeneity.example: An evaluation of a school meals programme finds a modest average effect on attendance, but separate estimates show a larger effect for girls than for boys. The sample was stratified by sex so that this difference could be detected.

hindu-rate-of-growth.definition: The 'Hindu rate of growth' is a tongue-in-cheek term coined by the economist Raj Krishna for the slow growth of India's economy, about 3.5 per cent a year, observed persistently from the 1950s to the late 1970s or 1980s. The term captured planners' frustration that growth seemed to return to this figure whatever they did. Practitioners meet it in discussions of India's economic history before the reforms. It refers to the period's policies and conditions and makes no claim about religion.
sources: Indian Economic Service, Arthapedia, Hindu rate of growth. https://ies.gov.in/arthapedia/concept/hindu-rate-growth
Basu, K. and Maertens, A., The Pattern and Causes of Economic Growth in India, Cornell CAE Working Paper 07-08 (2007). https://cae.economics.cornell.edu/07-08.pdf
hindu-rate-of-growth.example: Basu and Maertens note that India's growth fluctuated around 3.5 per cent a year in the 1950s, 60s and 70s, and averaged around 6 per cent between 1980 and 2005.

histogram.definition: A histogram is a chart that summarises the distribution of a single variable by grouping values into intervals (bins) and drawing adjacent bars whose heights show how many observations fall in each. It shows the centre, spread and skewness of the data, outliers, and whether there is more than one peak. Practitioners use histograms to understand the distribution of variables such as household income or test scores before analysing them further.
sources: NIST/SEMATECH, e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, section 1.3.3.14 Histogram. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/histogra.htm
histogram.example: A histogram of monthly household consumption in a district shows a long tail to the right, with most households bunched at low values and a few with much higher spending.

horizontal-devolution.definition: Horizontal devolution is the division of the states' share of central taxes among the states, using a formula recommended by the Finance Commission. The formula weights criteria such as population, area, forest cover, income distance and demographic performance. Practitioners use the term when analysing how much each state receives and how the choice of criteria affects poorer and richer states.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Explanatory Memorandum as to the Action Taken on the Recommendations Made by the Sixteenth Finance Commission, paragraph 5 (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/16fc.pdf
horizontal-devolution.example: The Sixteenth Finance Commission, covering 2026-27 to 2030-31, based the states' shares on population, demographic performance, area, forest, per capita income distance and each state's contribution to GDP. The Union government accepted the formula.

human-capital.definition: Human capital is the knowledge, skills and health that people build up over their lives and that enable them to be productive. Practitioners use the term when discussing investment in education, training, nutrition and health, which raise people's productivity and earnings and contribute to growth and job creation.
sources: World Bank, Human Capital (2024). https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/human-capital
human-capital.example: A programme that improves early childhood nutrition and the quality of primary schooling adds to human capital, because children grow up healthier and better able to learn and work.

human-development-index.definition: The Human Development Index (HDI), published by UNDP, is a summary measure of average achievement in three dimensions of human development. These are a long and healthy life (life expectancy at birth), knowledge (mean years of schooling for adults and expected years of schooling for children) and a decent standard of living (gross national income per capita, on a log scale). It is the geometric mean of the three normalised indices. It was created to show that people and their capabilities, and not economic growth alone, should be the criteria for judging development. It leaves out other aspects of human development, such as inequality, poverty and human security.
sources: UNDP Human Development Report Office, Human Development Index (HDI). https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/human-development-index
human-development-index.example: Two countries with similar GNI per capita can have quite different HDI values, which UNDP suggests can prompt questions about their policy priorities in health and education.

human-in-the-loop.definition: Human-in-the-loop describes an AI system that requires human interaction, typically so that a person reviews, approves or corrects the system's outputs before they take effect. Practitioners use the design in high-stakes settings such as health, welfare eligibility or fraud detection, where a human judgement is needed for accuracy and accountability.
sources: NIST, The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms, entry 'human-in-the-loop' (2023). https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/
human-in-the-loop.example: A system flags insurance claims that look unusual, and a trained officer reviews each flagged claim and decides whether to investigate before any payment is withheld.

ias.definition: The Indian Administrative Service (IAS) is an All India Service, common to the Union and the states, which Article 312 of the Constitution treats as a service created by Parliament. Its officers are recruited centrally and allotted to state cadres, and they serve in both state and Union governments, often heading district administrations and government departments. Practitioners working with government need to understand where IAS officers sit in the bureaucracy, because they usually lead the implementation of schemes in a district or department.
sources: Constitution of India, Article 312, Centre for Law and Policy Research. https://www.constitutionofindia.net/articles/article-312-all-india-services/
ias.example: A District Collector, who is usually an IAS officer, chairs district-level committees that review the progress of major schemes.

icds.definition: The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) is India's programme of services for young children, pregnant women and lactating mothers, delivered through anganwadi centres. It now runs as Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, which the Ministry of Women and Child Development describes as reorganising the erstwhile ICDS. Its Anganwadi Services package has six services, namely supplementary nutrition, pre-school non-formal education, nutrition and health education, immunisation, health check-ups and referral services. The last three are delivered through the National Health Mission. Practitioners work with ICDS when designing or supporting nutrition and early childhood interventions.
sources: Ministry of Women and Child Development, Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0. https://wcd.gov.in/pregnant-lactating-women-children/nutrition-mission-saksham-anganwadi-and-poshan-2-0
Ministry of Finance, Expenditure Profile 2026-27, Statement 13 (lists 'Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0 (Umbrella ICDS)'). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/eb/stat13.pdf
icds.example: An anganwadi centre provides supplementary nutrition to children aged six months to six years and to pregnant women and lactating mothers, and runs pre-school education for children aged three to six.

idiosyncratic-shock.definition: An idiosyncratic shock is an adverse event that hits a particular household or person, such as illness, injury, job loss or death of an earner, as opposed to a systemic (covariate) shock such as a drought, flood or price rise that hits many households at once. Because neighbours are not affected at the same time, communities can often help each other through idiosyncratic shocks with informal loans and support, though such arrangements are often inadequate for larger shocks or the most vulnerable. Practitioners use the distinction when designing social protection and insurance.
sources: World Bank, World Development Report 2014: Risk and Opportunity, chapter 4 (2013). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/16092
idiosyncratic-shock.example: When a daily wage earner falls ill and cannot work for a month, relatives and neighbours lend the household money for food and medicine. A drought that hits the whole village at once would leave the same neighbours unable to help.

impact.definition: Impact refers to the significant positive or negative, intended or unintended, higher-level effects of an intervention. Practitioners use this term when evaluating the outcomes of a project or program, such as the Janani Suraksha Yojana, to understand its broader influence on the community, beyond its immediate objectives.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, 2nd ed., entry 'Impact' (2023), trilingual edition published with IsDB (2024). https://www.isdb.org/sites/default/files/media/documents/2024-04/OECD%20Glossary%20of%20Key%20Evaluation%20Terms%20in%20Arabic%20English%20French.pdf
impact.example: A livelihoods programme's outputs are trainings held and loans given, and its outcomes are new enterprises started. Its impact would be lasting changes in household income and in women's say in household decisions, including any unintended effects such as children leaving school to help in the new enterprise.

impact-evaluation.definition: An impact evaluation assesses whether an intervention meets its higher-level goals and identifies its causal effects, that is, the changes in outcomes that can be attributed to the intervention. It answers the question of what difference the programme made by comparing actual outcomes with an estimate of what would have happened without it (the counterfactual). Impact evaluations may use experimental, quasi-experimental or non-experimental approaches, and the term is sometimes reserved for those with explicit counterfactual analysis. Practitioners use them to decide whether to continue, change or scale a programme.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, 2nd ed., entry 'Impact evaluation' (2023), trilingual edition published with IsDB (2024). https://www.isdb.org/sites/default/files/media/documents/2024-04/OECD%20Glossary%20of%20Key%20Evaluation%20Terms%20in%20Arabic%20English%20French.pdf
Gertler, P. J. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, 2nd ed., World Bank and IDB, chapter 1 (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
impact-evaluation.example: To estimate the effect of a school meals programme on attendance, evaluators compare schools randomly chosen to start the programme first with schools that start a year later.

implementation-gap.definition: An implementation gap is the difference between a policy or plan as written and what is actually delivered on the ground. Lant Pritchett describes the same divergence between de jure and de facto reality, arising when the agents of the state routinely do not carry out the tasks assigned to them. Practitioners use the term when diagnosing why a programme is not achieving its intended results, and look at causes such as inadequate resources, weak supervision, staff absence or lack of political priority.
sources: Pritchett, L., Is India a Flailing State?: Detours on the Four Lane Highway to Modernization, HKS Faculty Research Working Paper RWP09-013 (2009). https://www.hks.harvard.edu/publications/india-flailing-state-detours-four-lane-highway-modernization
implementation-gap.example: A scheme's guidelines require each health sub-centre to be staffed and open on fixed days, but a field visit finds many centres closed or without staff, so the services promised on paper do not reach patients.

inclusive-institutions.definition: Inclusive institutions are political and economic arrangements that allow broad participation and give most people a stake in the economy, through secure property rights, the rule of law and political rights. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson contrast them with extractive institutions, and argue that inclusive institutions create incentives to work and invest and are associated with long-run prosperity. Practitioners use the term when analysing why some societies grow and others stay poor.
sources: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2024 (2024). https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2024/popular-information/
inclusive-institutions.example: The laureates argue that colonies with many European settlers needed inclusive economic institutions that gave settlers incentives to work and invest, and that this in turn led to demands for wider political rights.

individual-forest-rights.definition: Individual forest rights (IFR) are rights recognised under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 for a forest dweller or family to hold and live on forest land they occupy for habitation or self-cultivation for livelihood (section 3(1)(a)). The land must have been occupied before 13 December 2005 and be under occupation when the Act came into force. The right is limited to the area actually occupied and in no case more than four hectares. It is heritable but cannot be sold or transferred, and is registered jointly in the names of both spouses. Practitioners use the term when helping forest-dwelling households secure tenure over the land they cultivate.
sources: Government of India, The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, sections 3(1)(a) and 4, as published by PRS Legislative Research. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_parliament/2006/the-scheduled-tribes-and-other-traditional-forest-dwellers-recognition-of-forest-rights-act-2006.pdf
individual-forest-rights.example: A tribal family that has cultivated two hectares of forest land since before 2005 files an IFR claim with the Gram Sabha, which verifies it and forwards it for approval. The title, if granted, is issued in the names of both husband and wife.

inference.definition: Inference is the stage of machine learning in which a trained model is applied to a task, for example a classifier assigning a new record to a category. Practitioners use the term for the deployment step after training, when the model is run on new data such as fresh survey records to produce predictions that inform decisions.
sources: NIST, The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms, entry 'inference' (2023). https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/
inference.example: After training a model on last year's survey to predict which households are poor, a team runs it on newly collected records to produce a predicted poverty status for each household.

information-asymmetry.definition: Information asymmetry is a situation in which one party to a transaction knows more than the other, for example a seller who knows the quality of a used car better than the buyer, or a borrower who knows their own creditworthiness better than the lender. The theory of markets with asymmetric information, for which Akerlof, Spence and Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel Prize, shows that it can make markets work badly or not at all. Practitioners use the concept when analysing credit, insurance and labour markets and the design of public programmes.
sources: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Information for the Public: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2001, Markets with Asymmetric Information (2001). https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2001/popular-information/
information-asymmetry.example: A lender who cannot tell careful borrowers from risky ones and charges everyone a high interest rate risks attracting mainly borrowers with poor repayment prospects.

information-commission.definition: An Information Commission is a statutory body set up under the Right to Information Act, 2005. The Central Information Commission is constituted under section 12 and each State Information Commission under section 15. A Commission hears second appeals against the decisions of First Appellate Authorities, which must be filed within ninety days (section 19(3)), and complaints under section 18, for example where a request was refused or no Public Information Officer had been appointed. Practitioners turn to it when an RTI request has been denied or ignored and a first appeal has not resolved the matter.
sources: Government of India, The Right to Information Act, 2005, sections 12, 15, 18 and 19 (as published by the Central Information Commission). https://cic.gov.in/sites/default/files/RTI-Act_English.pdf
information-commission.example: After a first appeal to the department's appellate officer brings no reply, an applicant files a second appeal with the State Information Commission within ninety days, asking it to direct the department to supply the records.

informed-consent.definition: Informed consent is a person's voluntary agreement to take part in research or data collection after being given, and understanding, the information relevant to that decision. India's ICMR ethical guidelines describe the process as having three parts, namely giving potential participants relevant information, making sure they understand it, and ensuring that their participation is voluntary. Information should be in simple terms and in a language the person understands. Practitioners must obtain it before collecting data from people, and in low-literacy settings the guidelines call for an impartial literate witness.
sources: Indian Council of Medical Research, National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, section 2.2 (2017). https://ethics.ncdirindia.org/asset/pdf/ICMR_National_Ethical_Guidelines.pdf
informed-consent.example: Before a household survey, an enumerator reads the consent form aloud in the local language, explains the purpose, risks and the right to refuse or stop at any time, and records consent in front of an impartial witness when the respondent cannot read.

institutions.definition: Institutions are the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction, in Douglass North's definition. They include informal constraints such as customs, traditions and codes of conduct, and formal rules such as constitutions, laws and property rights. By reducing uncertainty in exchange they affect transaction and production costs and so shape economic performance. Practitioners use the term when analysing how rules and norms shape the behaviour of people and organisations and the results of programmes.
sources: North, D. C., Institutions, Journal of Economic Perspectives 5(1) (1991). https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.5.1.97
institutions.example: Two villages receive the same irrigation scheme, but in one the water users' association has clear rules for sharing water and sanctions that members respect, while in the other it has neither. The difference in institutions helps explain why the scheme works in one village and not the other.

instrumental-variables.definition: Instrumental variables (IV) is a method for estimating a causal effect when treatment is not randomly assigned or when not everyone complies with their assignment. It uses an external source of variation, the instrument, that affects whether a unit takes part in the programme but is outside the participant's control and unrelated to their characteristics, so that it affects the outcome only through participation. Practitioners use IV for programmes with voluntary enrolment, imperfect compliance or universal coverage, and the result is only as credible as the case that the instrument has no other route to the outcome.
sources: Gertler, P. J. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, 2nd ed., World Bank and IDB, chapter 5 'Instrumental Variables' (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
instrumental-variables.example: In a randomised evaluation where some households offered a programme do not enrol, the random offer itself can be used as an instrument for enrolment, giving an estimate of the effect on those who enrolled because they were offered it.

internal-validity.definition: Internal validity is the extent to which an evaluation's estimate of a programme's effect is free of other confounding factors, so that it can be attributed to the programme. An evaluation is internally valid if its comparison group gives an accurate estimate of the counterfactual, that is, of what would have happened to participants without the programme. Practitioners look for it when judging whether an evaluation's findings can be trusted as causal. It is distinct from external validity, which concerns whether the results apply to other people or places.
sources: Gertler, P. J. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, 2nd ed., World Bank and IDB, chapter 4 (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
internal-validity.example: An evaluation that randomly assigns villages to receive a nutrition programme now or a year later has high internal validity, because random assignment makes the two groups similar in everything except the programme. A study comparing villages that chose to join with villages that did not has lower internal validity, because the joining villages may differ in other ways.

interoperability.definition: Interoperability is the ability of software or hardware systems or components to work together and exchange and use data with minimal effort by the user. Practitioners use the term when linking data systems, for example health, education and social protection records, so that information collected once can be used by other programmes without manual re-entry.
sources: NIST, The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms, entry 'interoperability' (2023). https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/
interoperability.example: A state links its school enrolment database and its scholarship payment system through a shared student identifier and an agreed data format, so that eligible students are identified automatically without re-entering their details.

job-card.definition: A job card is the document issued to a rural household registered under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 (MGNREGA). The Gram Panchayat registers a household on application and issues a job card listing its adult members with their photographs. Every adult named on it can apply for unskilled manual work, and work must be provided within fifteen days of an application. The Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-G RAM G), which came into force on 1 July 2026 and repeals MGNREGA from a date the Union government notifies, provides for a Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Card in its place. Practitioners use job card records to check whether households receive the work and wages they are entitled to.
sources: Government of India, The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, Schedule II, as published by PRS Legislative Research. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_parliament/2005/the-national-rural-employment-guarantee-act-2005.pdf

Government of India, The Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (No. 36 of 2025), as published by PRS Legislative Research. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/bills_parliament/2025/Viksit_Bharat_G_RAM_G_Act_2025.pdf
job-card.example: A household in Rajasthan applies to its Gram Panchayat for registration and receives a job card naming its three adult members, each of whom can then apply for work under the scheme.

keyboard-navigation.definition: Keyboard navigation is the ability to use all the functions of a website or digital tool through a keyboard or keyboard interface alone, without a mouse. WCAG success criterion 2.1.1 (Level A) requires that all functionality be operable through a keyboard interface, except functions that depend on the path of a movement such as freehand drawing. Many people rely on it, including blind users and some people with mobility impairments. Practitioners must provide it when building dashboards, data tools and online forms.
sources: W3C, Understanding WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A). https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/keyboard.html
keyboard-navigation.example: A district dashboard lets users move between filters and charts with the Tab key and open each chart's data table with Enter, so a screen reader user can reach every figure without a mouse.

knowledge-management.definition: Knowledge management is the process or approach through which organisations capture, share, retain and use knowledge to achieve their goals. Practitioners use it to document lessons from past projects, successes and failures alike, so that they inform future programme design and implementation.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, 2nd ed., entry 'Knowledge management' (2023), trilingual edition published with IsDB (2024). https://www.isdb.org/sites/default/files/media/documents/2024-04/OECD%20Glossary%20of%20Key%20Evaluation%20Terms%20in%20Arabic%20English%20French.pdf
knowledge-management.example: After each project closes, an NGO holds a review, records the main lessons in a searchable library, and requires new project proposals to show which past lessons they have drawn on.

land-tenure-security.definition: Land tenure security is the certainty that a person's rights to land will be recognised by others and protected when challenged. People with insecure tenure risk losing their rights to competing claims or eviction. FAO notes that tenure security cannot be measured directly and is to a large extent what people perceive it to be, and that it depends on how long rights last relative to the time needed to recover an investment. Secure tenure matters for food security, livelihoods and the incentive to invest in land. Practitioners use the term in work on rural development, forest rights and urban housing.
sources: FAO, Land tenure and rural development, FAO Land Tenure Studies 3, paragraphs 3.31 and 3.32 (2002). https://www.fao.org/4/y4307e/y4307e05.htm
land-tenure-security.example: A farmer who can use a plot only for a single season has no reason to plant trees or build an irrigation channel on it, because she may not be there to benefit. A farmer with long-term recognised rights to the same plot has that reason.

large-language-model.definition: A large language model (LLM) is a language model built with deep learning and trained on very large collections of text. Generative LLMs produce text, such as answers to questions or drafts of documents. Practitioners in the development sector use LLMs to help draft reports, summarise documents or answer questions about them, and need to check their outputs, because the text they produce can be fluent and still wrong.
sources: NIST, The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms, entry 'large language model (LLM)' (2023). https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/
large-language-model.example: An evaluation team uses an LLM to produce first summaries of a hundred interview transcripts, then checks each summary against the transcript before using it in analysis.

larr-act-2013.definition: The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (No. 30 of 2013), often called the LARR or RFCTLARR Act, governs compulsory acquisition of land in India. Its stated aim is a humane, participative, informed and transparent process for acquiring land, carried out in consultation with local self-government institutions and Gram Sabhas, with just and fair compensation and adequate rehabilitation and resettlement for affected families. Practitioners use it when working with communities affected by infrastructure, industrial or urban projects that need land.
sources: Government of India, The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Gazette of India (27 September 2013), hosted by the Department of Land Resources. https://cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in/s3d69116f8b0140cdeb1f99a4d5096ffe4/uploads/2024/02/20240222103134857.pdf
larr-act-2013.example: When land is to be acquired for a road project, affected families and the Gram Sabha are consulted under the Act, and families are entitled to compensation and to rehabilitation and resettlement under its provisions.

logframe.definition: A logframe (logical framework) is a management tool used to improve the design of interventions, most often at project level. It sets out the intervention's strategic elements (inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact) and the causal links between them, together with indicators and the assumptions or risks that may affect success. It is commonly laid out as a matrix with columns for indicators, means of verification and assumptions. Practitioners use it for planning, monitoring and evaluation, and to make explicit the risks and assumptions behind a project.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, 2nd ed., entry 'Logical framework (Log frame)' (2023), trilingual edition published with IsDB (2024). https://www.isdb.org/sites/default/files/media/documents/2024-04/OECD%20Glossary%20of%20Key%20Evaluation%20Terms%20in%20Arabic%20English%20French.pdf
logframe.example: A water project's logframe states that building handpumps (output) is expected to increase the use of safe water (outcome) and reduce diarrhoea among children (impact), on the assumption that communities maintain the pumps, and names the indicator and data source for each level.

lorenz-curve.definition: The Lorenz curve is a graph of inequality that plots the cumulative share of income or consumption (on the vertical axis) against the cumulative share of the population, ordered from poorest to richest (on the horizontal axis). A 45-degree line represents perfect equality, and the further the curve sags below it, the more unequal the distribution. The Gini index is derived from it as the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve. Practitioners use it to show and compare how income or consumption is distributed.
sources: World Bank, Poverty and Inequality Platform Methodology Handbook, section 4.3 'Inequality measures'. https://datanalytics.worldbank.org/PIP-Methodology/surveyestimates.html
lorenz-curve.example: If the poorest half of a district's households account for a fifth of its total consumption, the district's Lorenz curve passes through the point (50 per cent of households, 20 per cent of consumption), well below the line of equality.

machine-learning.definition: Machine learning (ML) is a branch of artificial intelligence concerned with systems that learn from data to perform a task without being explicitly programmed for it. Learning here means optimising a model's parameters on training data. Practitioners use ML to find patterns in large datasets and make predictions, for example of poverty or crop yields, and must check that those predictions are accurate and fair for the people affected.
sources: NIST, The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms, entry 'machine learning' (2023). https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/
machine-learning.example: A team trains a model on survey data that link household assets to measured consumption, then uses it to predict consumption for households where only asset data are available.

microfinance.definition: Microfinance refers to financial services for low-income households and small businesses that are poorly served by conventional banks, including small loans, savings and insurance. In India the RBI defines a microfinance loan as a collateral-free loan to a household with annual income up to ₹3,00,000, whatever its purpose and whether it is given physically or digitally, and requires lenders to keep repayments within a limit set against household income. Practitioners use microfinance in programmes on livelihoods, women's economic participation and rural development.
sources: Reserve Bank of India, Master Direction: Regulatory Framework for Microfinance Loans, Directions 2022 (as amended). https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasDirections.aspx?id=12256
microfinance.example: A woman in a rural household with an annual income of ₹1,80,000 takes a collateral-free loan of ₹40,000 from a microfinance institution to buy a sewing machine. Under the RBI's rules this counts as a microfinance loan.

mid-day-meal.definition: The Mid-Day Meal scheme, formally the National Programme of Mid-Day Meals in Schools and now called PM POSHAN (Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman), is a centrally sponsored scheme that provides meals to children in school. Its primary objective is to improve the nutritional status of children studying in classes I to VIII in eligible schools. It is a rights-based scheme under the National Food Security Act, 2013, which entitles children aged six to fourteen to a free nutritious meal through schools. Practitioners use the term in work on child nutrition, school attendance and learning.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Notes on Demands for Grants 2026-27, Department of School Education and Literacy, item 13 (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/eb/sbe25.pdf
Department of Food and Public Distribution, National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013, NFSA portal. https://nfsa.gov.in/portal/nfsa-act
mid-day-meal.example: A primary school serves a cooked lunch on every school day to enrolled children, and the head teacher records the number of meals served for reporting under PM POSHAN.

missing-data.definition: Missing data are values that should have been recorded but are absent from a dataset. How they are handled can bias results. Statisticians distinguish data missing completely at random (the chance of being missing is the same for every case), missing at random (the chance is the same within groups defined by observed data) and missing not at random (the chance depends on unknown reasons, often the missing value itself). Dropping incomplete cases (listwise deletion) is common but can distort results unless data are missing completely at random, and methods such as multiple imputation are used instead. Practitioners must decide, and document, whether to show gaps, impute values or exclude cases.
sources: van Buuren, S., Flexible Imputation of Missing Data, 2nd ed., sections 1.1 to 1.3 (2018). https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html
missing-data.example: In a household survey, richer households refuse the income question more often than poorer ones. Simply dropping those households would understate average income, because the data are not missing at random.

model.definition: The mathematical representation learned from training data. A 'trained model' contains the patterns discovered and can make predictions on new data.
sources: NIST, The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms, entry 'model' (2023). https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/
model.example: A random forest model trained to predict crop yields from satellite imagery.

model-drift.definition: Model drift is the decline in a model's performance over time as real-world conditions move away from those in its training data. It includes data drift, where the inputs change, and concept drift, where the relationship between the inputs and the outcome changes. Practitioners monitor deployed models and retrain them when drift is detected.
sources: NIST, The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms, entries 'model decay', 'concept drift' and 'data drift' (2023). https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/
model-drift.example: A poverty model trained on data from 2015 becomes less accurate as prices, jobs and asset ownership change, so its predictions drift away from what new surveys find.

moral-hazard.definition: Moral hazard is the change in behaviour that occurs when someone is protected from the full consequences of their actions and those actions cannot be fully observed by the party bearing the cost. Insurance is the classic case. A fully insured person may become more careless, which is why insurers use deductibles and co-payments. Practitioners consider it when designing insurance, credit and incentive schemes.
sources: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2016, Contract theory (2016). https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2016/popular-information/
moral-hazard.example: An insurer pays only part of the cost of each claim, so that policyholders still bear some loss from an accident and have a reason to take care.

most-significant-change.definition: The Most Significant Change (MSC) technique is a form of participatory monitoring and evaluation developed by Rick Davies. It involves collecting stories of significant change from the field and having panels of stakeholders or staff systematically select the most significant of them, discussing why each change matters. It uses no pre-defined indicators, so it can reveal unexpected outcomes and the values that different stakeholders hold.
sources: Davies, R. and Dart, J., The 'Most Significant Change' (MSC) Technique: A Guide to Its Use (2005). https://www.mande.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2005/MSCGuide.pdf
most-significant-change.example: In a livelihoods programme, field staff collect stories of change from participants every quarter, and a district panel reads them aloud, chooses the most significant and records its reasons. Over time the selected stories show what participants and staff value most.

muster-roll.definition: A muster roll is the official record of workers present at a worksite under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005. The Act requires the Programme Officer to supply each Gram Panchayat with muster rolls for the works it executes, and requires the Gram Panchayat to make muster rolls available to the Gram Sabha for social audits, which makes them a central document for accountability. The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, in force since 1 July 2026, keeps the same requirements.
sources: Government of India, The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, sections 16 and 17, as published by PRS Legislative Research. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_parliament/2005/the-national-rural-employment-guarantee-act-2005.pdf

Government of India, The Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025, as published by PRS Legislative Research. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/bills_parliament/2025/Viksit_Bharat_G_RAM_G_Act_2025.pdf
muster-roll.example: During a social audit, residents read out the names on a work's muster roll and check them against who actually worked, to find names of people who were not present.

named-entity-recognition.definition: Named entity recognition (NER) is the task of finding spans of text that are proper names and tagging each with its type. The most common types are person, location, organisation and geo-political entity, and the term is often extended to dates, times and amounts. It is hard partly because the boundaries of a name can be ambiguous and the same name can refer to different kinds of thing.
sources: Jurafsky, D. and Martin, J. H., Speech and Language Processing, 3rd ed. draft, chapter 18 'Sequence Labeling for Parts of Speech and Named Entities' (2026). https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/18.pdf
named-entity-recognition.example: Extracting the names of villages, districts and organisations from thousands of field reports so that incidents can be mapped and counted by place.

natural-language-processing.definition: Natural language processing (NLP) is the field concerned with getting computers to process, analyse and generate human language, whether spoken, written or signed. Today much of it is done with language models. Practitioners use NLP to analyse text at scale, for example open-ended survey answers, field reports or grievance records.
sources: NIST, The Language of Trustworthy AI: An In-Depth Glossary of Terms, entry 'natural language processing' (2023). https://airc.nist.gov/glossary/
Jurafsky, D. and Martin, J. H., Speech and Language Processing, 3rd ed. draft, chapter 1 (2026). https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/1.pdf
natural-language-processing.example: Analysing thousands of open-ended survey responses to identify common themes, with a researcher checking a sample of the coded answers by hand.

nfsa.definition: The National Food Security Act, 2013 (NFSA), enacted on 5 July 2013, gives a legal entitlement to subsidised foodgrains through the Targeted Public Distribution System to up to 75 per cent of India's rural population and 50 per cent of its urban population, about two-thirds of the population. Foodgrains were to be supplied at ₹3, ₹2 and ₹1 per kg for rice, wheat and coarse grains for an initial three years, after which the Union government fixes the prices. The eldest woman of a household aged 18 or above is its head for issuing ration cards. The Act also entitles pregnant women, lactating mothers and children aged six months to fourteen years to free meals through anganwadi centres and schools, and pregnant women and lactating mothers to a cash maternity benefit.
sources: Department of Food and Public Distribution, National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013, NFSA portal. https://nfsa.gov.in/portal/nfsa-act
nfsa.example: Out of a maximum coverage of 81.34 crore persons, the Department of Food and Public Distribution reports that around 80 crore are covered under the NFSA.

nighttime-lights.definition: Nighttime lights are satellite measurements of artificial light visible from space at night. Researchers use them as a proxy for economic activity and electrification, especially where official statistics are weak or are not available for small areas. Henderson, Storeygard and Weil showed that night lights can be combined with official figures to improve estimates of income growth and to measure growth for regions below or across national borders.
sources: Henderson, J. V., Storeygard, A. and Weil, D. N., Measuring Economic Growth from Outer Space, American Economic Review 102(2) (2012). https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.102.2.994
nighttime-lights.example: A study uses changes in the brightness of night lights between two years to estimate economic growth in districts for which no district income figures are published.
