normalization.definition: Normalisation means transforming data to a common scale so that values measured in different units or magnitudes can be compared or combined. A common method is min-max scaling, which places each value between 0 and 1 using chosen minimum and maximum values. Practitioners normalise indicators before combining them into a composite index, and must report the method because the choice affects the results.
sources: UNDP, Human Development Report 2025, Technical notes (2025). https://hdr.undp.org/sites/default/files/2025_HDR/hdr2025_technical_notes.pdf
normalization.example: The Human Development Index turns life expectancy, schooling and income into dimension indices between 0 and 1, each calculated as the actual value minus a minimum, divided by the maximum minus the minimum, before combining them.

nregamgnrega.definition: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 (MGNREGA, originally NREGA) guarantees at least one hundred days of wage employment in each financial year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work. If work is not provided within fifteen days of an application, the state government must pay an unemployment allowance. The Gram Sabha conducts social audits of works. In December 2025 Parliament passed the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-G RAM G), which raises the guarantee to 125 days, changes the funding to a centrally sponsored scheme shared between the Union and the states, and repeals MGNREGA from a date the Union government notifies. The new Act came into force on 1 July 2026.
sources: Government of India, The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, as published by PRS Legislative Research. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_parliament/2005/the-national-rural-employment-guarantee-act-2005.pdf

PRS Legislative Research, The Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) VB-G RAM G Bill, 2025, bill summary. https://prsindia.org/billtrack/the-viksit-bharat-%E2%80%93-guarantee-for-rozgar-and-ajeevika-mission-gramin-vb-%E2%80%93-g-ram-g-bill-2025

Government of India, The Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025, section 37. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/bills_parliament/2025/Viksit_Bharat_G_RAM_G_Act_2025.pdf
nregamgnrega.example: A rural household registered under the scheme applies for work in the lean season, and its members are given work on a village water conservation project within fifteen days.

nutrition.definition: Nutrition is the intake and use of food and nutrients, and good nutrition is a critical part of health and development. WHO links better nutrition to improved infant, child and maternal health, stronger immunity, lower risk of non-communicable diseases and greater productivity. Malnutrition covers deficiencies, excesses or imbalances in a person's intake of energy or nutrients. It includes undernutrition (wasting, stunting and underweight), micronutrient deficiencies or excess, and overweight and obesity. Stunting holds children back from reaching their physical and cognitive potential, which is why nutrition matters for human capital.
sources: WHO, Nutrition, health topic page. https://www.who.int/health-topics/nutrition
WHO, Malnutrition, fact sheet. https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malnutrition
nutrition.example: WHO estimates that in 2022, 149 million children under five were stunted (too short for their age) and 45 million were wasted (too thin for their height).

off-budget-financing.definition: Off-budget financing is spending for government purposes that is paid for through borrowing by other bodies, such as public sector undertakings or special purpose entities, with the government bearing the repayment, so that the borrowing does not appear in the government's own budget or headline fiscal deficit. It makes the reported deficit understate the government's true borrowing. India's Union budget has disclosed such borrowing as Extra Budgetary Resources since 2019, and the Sixteenth Finance Commission has recommended that states stop off-budget borrowing altogether.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Budget Speech 2021-22, paragraph 143 and Annexure VI (2021). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/budget2021-22/doc/Budget_Speech.pdf
Ministry of Finance, Explanatory Memorandum as to the Action Taken on the Recommendations Made by the Sixteenth Finance Commission, paragraph 26 (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/16fc.pdf
off-budget-financing.example: Until 2020-21 the Food Corporation of India borrowed from the National Small Savings Fund to meet food subsidy costs. The Budget of February 2021 discontinued this NSSF loan to FCI and provided for the subsidy in the budget instead.

relevance.definition: The extent to which the objectives and design of an intervention respond to the needs, policies and priorities of beneficiaries, the country, partner institutions and the wider world, and continue to do so if circumstances change.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, Second Edition (2023). https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
relevance.example: An IT training program had low relevance when assessment showed beneficiaries prioritized agricultural skills over computer literacy.

reliability.definition: The extent to which the same measurement process produces consistent results across different times, locations, or observers.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, Second Edition (2023). https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
reliability.example: Different enumerators classifying the same household sanitation facility differently indicates low inter-rater reliability.

results-chain.definition: The causal sequence connecting program resources to ultimate impact: Inputs → Activities → Outputs → Outcomes → Impact.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, Second Edition (2023). https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
results-chain.example: In a vaccination program: funding and vaccines (inputs) → immunization campaigns (activities) → children vaccinated (outputs) → increased immunity (outcomes) → reduced disease burden (impact).

rbm.definition: Results-Based Management, management strategy focusing on achieving defined results (outputs, outcomes, impacts) rather than just implementing activities.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, Second Edition (2023). https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
rbm.example: A programme sets out its expected outputs, outcomes and impacts at the design stage, and its managers use monitoring data on progress towards them to make decisions and report to funders.

summative-evaluation.definition: An evaluation conducted at the end of an intervention, or of a phase of it, to determine how far the expected outcomes were achieved. It gives information about the worth or significance of the intervention.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, Second Edition (2023). https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
summative-evaluation.example: The summative evaluation concluded the program achieved 3 of 5 objectives and provided recommendations for future programming.

sustainability.definition: The extent to which the net benefits of an intervention continue, or are likely to continue. Assessing it involves the financial, economic, social, environmental and institutional capacities needed to sustain those benefits over time.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, Second Edition (2023). https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
sustainability.example: Water committees continued functioning 3 years post-project because the program invested in building local repair capacity and fee collection systems.

validity.definition: The extent to which data measures what it claims to measure, whether the indicator actually captures the intended concept.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, Second Edition (2023). https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
validity.example: Measuring 'empowerment' by counting women's group meetings attended has low validity, because attendance doesn't equal empowerment.

process-evaluation.definition: Assessment of how a program is implemented, whether activities are delivered as planned and what contextual factors affect delivery.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, Second Edition (2023). https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
process-evaluation.example: Process evaluation found that only 60% of planned home visits occurred because CHWs lacked transport during monsoon season.

ordinance.definition: A law made by the President under Article 123 when both Houses of Parliament are not in session and the President is satisfied that immediate action is needed. It has the same force as an Act of Parliament, must be laid before both Houses, and ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless replaced by an Act. It ends sooner if both Houses pass resolutions disapproving it, and the President may withdraw it at any time.
sources: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, The Constitution of India, as on 1 May 2026 (2026). https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/c9fe9c9b6840524844316f74bb1c556c.pdf
ordinance.example: When Parliament is not in session, the government may bring a change into force by ordinance and then introduce a Bill to replace it when Parliament meets.

seventh-schedule.definition: Constitutional schedule dividing legislative competence into Union List, State List, and Concurrent List. Fundamental to understanding which level of government can act on any policy question.
sources: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, The Constitution of India, as on 1 May 2026 (2026). https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/c9fe9c9b6840524844316f74bb1c556c.pdf
seventh-schedule.example: A policy analyst working on water must check the Schedule. Water supplies, irrigation and canals are entry 17 of the State List, but this is subject to entry 56 of the Union List, under which Parliament may declare Union control over the regulation and development of inter-State rivers to be in the public interest.

state-list.definition: List II of the Seventh Schedule, the subjects on which State Legislatures have exclusive power to make laws under Article 246(3). Its entries are numbered up to 66, and seven of them have since been omitted by amendment. It includes police, public health and sanitation, agriculture, water and land. Parliament may legislate on a State List subject in the national interest under Article 249, but only after the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting.
sources: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, The Constitution of India, as on 1 May 2026 (2026). https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/c9fe9c9b6840524844316f74bb1c556c.pdf
state-list.example: Police and public health are State List subjects, so the main laws and spending on them come from state governments.

union-list.definition: List I of the Seventh Schedule, the subjects on which Parliament has exclusive power to make laws under Article 246(1). Its entries are numbered 1 to 97, with a few inserted and omitted by amendment. It includes defence, foreign affairs, railways, banking and taxes on income other than agricultural income.
sources: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, The Constitution of India, as on 1 May 2026 (2026). https://www.legislative.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/07/c9fe9c9b6840524844316f74bb1c556c.pdf
union-list.example: Banking is entry 45 of the Union List, so only Parliament can make laws on banking.

permissible-works.definition: The categories of work that may be taken up under India's rural employment guarantee, listed in Schedule I of the law. The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, in force since 1 July 2026, is replacing the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, which it repeals from a date the Central Government notifies. The new Act groups works into four categories. These are water-related works, core rural infrastructure, livelihood-related infrastructure, and works to mitigate extreme weather events and prepare for disasters. The Act also allows maintenance of rural public assets, works for individual beneficiaries under notified central schemes, and other public works the Central Government notifies.
sources: India Code, The Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (Act No. 36 of 2025). https://indiacode.gov.in/items/63b87434-40a1-4eaf-a44e-adcc29215670

Press Information Bureau, Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (11 May 2026). https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2026/may/doc2026511867601.pdf
permissible-works.example: Check dams, recharge pits and the rejuvenation of ponds fall under the water-related category of works.

unemployment-allowance.definition: A daily cash allowance due to a rural employment applicant who is not given work within fifteen days of applying, or of the date from which work was sought in an advance application. Under the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, in force since 1 July 2026, the rate is set by the State Government but cannot be less than one-fourth of the notified wage rate for the first thirty days in a financial year and one-half thereafter. The State Government bears the cost.
sources: India Code, The Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (Act No. 36 of 2025), and section 22(8). https://indiacode.gov.in/items/63b87434-40a1-4eaf-a44e-adcc29215670

Press Information Bureau, Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (11 May 2026). https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2026/may/doc2026511867601.pdf

wage-material-ratio.definition: The limit on how much of the spending on rural employment guarantee works may go on materials. Under Schedule I of the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, in force since 1 July 2026, the cost of the material component of all works must not exceed forty per cent at the district level. The rule is commonly described as a 60 to 40 ratio of wages to materials.
sources: India Code, The Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (Act No. 36 of 2025), Schedule I, paragraph 20. https://indiacode.gov.in/items/63b87434-40a1-4eaf-a44e-adcc29215670

social-audit.definition: A public check, carried out by the community, of the records of a government programme against what happened on the ground. Under India's rural employment guarantee law the Gram Sabha must conduct regular social audits of all works in the Gram Panchayat, and the Gram Panchayat must give it the muster rolls, bills, vouchers, measurement books, sanction orders and other records needed.
sources: India Code, The Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (Act No. 36 of 2025), https://indiacode.gov.in/items/63b87434-40a1-4eaf-a44e-adcc29215670
social-audit.example: At a social audit, villagers compare the names on a muster roll with who actually worked on the site.

self-targeting.definition: A targeting method in which a programme is open to everyone but is designed so that the poorest choose to take part and the better off do not, because the private costs of taking part differ between them. Examples include low wages on public works, a requirement to queue, in-kind benefits of lower quality, and service points located where the poor are concentrated.
sources: World Bank, Coady, Grosh and Hoddinott, Targeting of Transfers in Developing Countries: Review of Lessons and Experience (2004). https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/464231468779449856/pdf/302300PAPER0Targeting0of0transfers.pdf
self-targeting.example: A public works scheme that pays a low wage for unskilled manual work attracts mainly people with few better options, without any means test. The World Bank review cites Maharashtra's Employment Guarantee Scheme as an example.

proxy-means-test.definition: A targeting method that predicts poverty using observable household characteristics (assets, housing) as proxies for income.
sources: World Bank, Coady, Grosh and Hoddinott, Targeting of Transfers in Developing Countries: Review of Lessons and Experience (2004). https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/464231468779449856/pdf/302300PAPER0Targeting0of0transfers.pdf
proxy-means-test.example: A formula scoring households based on roof material, water source, and asset ownership.

targeting.definition: Methods for directing programme benefits to intended recipients. They include individual assessment (means tests, proxy means tests and community-based targeting), categorical targeting such as geographic or age-based eligibility, and self-selection.
sources: World Bank, Coady, Grosh and Hoddinott, Targeting of Transfers in Developing Countries: Review of Lessons and Experience (2004). https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/464231468779449856/pdf/302300PAPER0Targeting0of0transfers.pdf
targeting.example: A cash transfer may combine geographic targeting of poorer districts with a proxy means test of households inside them.

public-information-officer.definition: An officer designated by a public authority under section 5 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 to provide information to people who request it. The officer must provide the information or reject the request within thirty days, or within forty-eight hours where the information concerns a person's life or liberty. The Information Commission may impose a penalty of 250 rupees a day on the officer for delay or refusal without reasonable cause, up to a total of 25,000 rupees.
sources: Central Information Commission, Right to Information Act, 2005 (Act No. 22 of 2005), as modified up to 1 February 2011. https://cic.gov.in/sites/default/files/RTI-Act_English.pdf

proactive-disclosure.definition: RTI provision requiring government offices to publish key information without waiting for requests. Suo motu disclosure under Section 4.
sources: Central Information Commission, Right to Information Act, 2005 (Act No. 22 of 2005), https://cic.gov.in/sites/default/files/RTI-Act_English.pdf

right-to-information.definition: RTI Act 2005 gives citizens the right to request information from public authorities, with 30-day response deadline and penalties for non-compliance.
sources: Central Information Commission, Right to Information Act, 2005 (Act No. 22 of 2005). https://cic.gov.in/sites/default/files/RTI-Act_English.pdf

rti-act.definition: The Right to Information Act, 2005. It gives all citizens the right to information held by public authorities. A Public Information Officer must provide the information or reject the request with reasons within thirty days, and the Information Commissions hear appeals and complaints and can impose penalties.
sources: Central Information Commission, Right to Information Act, 2005 (Act No. 22 of 2005). https://cic.gov.in/sites/default/files/RTI-Act_English.pdf
rti-act.example: A citizen can file an RTI request with a block office asking for copies of the muster rolls for a local works project.

priority-household.definition: One of the two categories of households entitled to foodgrains under the National Food Security Act, 2013, alongside Antyodaya Anna Yojana households. States and Union Territories identify priority households using their own criteria. Each member is entitled to 5 kg of foodgrains a month, which the Central Government has provided free of cost since 1 January 2023, extended for five years from 1 January 2024.
sources: Press Information Bureau, Securing Every Plate: India's Multi-Faceted Mission to Ensure Food and Nutritional Equity for 81 Crore Citizens (October 2025). https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2025/oct/doc20251015667601.pdf

public-distribution-system.definition: The system through which the Central and State governments distribute foodgrains at affordable prices to ration card holders through Fair Price Shops. Under the National Food Security Act, 2013 it runs as the Targeted Public Distribution System. The Centre procures, allocates and moves grain to Food Corporation of India depots, and states identify beneficiaries, issue ration cards and supervise about 5.4 lakh Fair Price Shops. Reforms include digitised ration cards, Aadhaar seeding, ePoS devices for biometric authentication at the shop, and One Nation One Ration Card portability.
sources: Press Information Bureau, Securing Every Plate: India's Multi-Faceted Mission to Ensure Food and Nutritional Equity for 81 Crore Citizens (October 2025). https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2025/oct/doc20251015667601.pdf
public-distribution-system.example: Under One Nation One Ration Card, a migrant worker can collect entitled grain from any Fair Price Shop in the country using biometric authentication.

pesa-act.definition: The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996, in force from 24 December 1996. It extends panchayat provisions to Fifth Schedule areas and gives special powers to the Gram Sabha. These include safeguarding the traditions, customs, community resources and customary dispute resolution of the people, approving development plans and identifying beneficiaries. The Gram Sabha or Panchayat must be consulted on land acquisition and resettlement, must make recommendations before mineral licences or leases are granted, and is to be given ownership of minor forest produce and powers to prevent land alienation.
sources: Ministry of Panchayati Raj via Press Information Bureau, Concept Note on The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) (2021). https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2021/nov/doc2021111811.pdf
pesa-act.example: Before land in a Scheduled Area is acquired for a project, the Gram Sabha or Panchayat at the appropriate level must be consulted.

primary-deficit.definition: Fiscal deficit minus interest payments. It shows how much of the government's borrowing goes to meet expenses other than interest on past debt.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Budget at a Glance 2026-27 (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/Budget_at_Glance/budget_at_a_glance.pdf
Ministry of Finance, Union Budget 2018-19 brochure, Budget Glossary (2018). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/budget2018-2019/NewIndiaBudget/images/union-budget-2018-brochure.pdf
primary-deficit.example: A high-debt government may have a large fiscal deficit primarily due to interest payments on old debt, the primary deficit reveals whether current policy is adding to that stock.

revenue-deficit.definition: Revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Measures how much current operating expenditure exceeds current income, borrowing to fund day-to-day expenses rather than capital investment.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Budget at a Glance 2026-27 (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/Budget_at_Glance/budget_at_a_glance.pdf
revenue-deficit.example: In the Budget Estimates for 2026-27, the Union government's revenue deficit is 5,92,344 crore rupees, about 1.5 per cent of GDP, so part of its borrowing pays for revenue spending.

revised-estimate.definition: A mid-year review of likely expenditure for the current financial year, presented alongside the next year's Budget Estimates. Revised Estimates are not voted by Parliament, so they do not by themselves authorise spending. Any additional amount must be approved by Parliament or through a re-appropriation order.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Union Budget 2018-19 brochure, Budget Glossary (2018). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/budget2018-2019/NewIndiaBudget/images/union-budget-2018-brochure.pdf
Ministry of Finance, Budget at a Glance 2026-27 (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/Budget_at_Glance/budget_at_a_glance.pdf
revised-estimate.example: The Budget at a Glance for 2026-27 shows the Revised Estimates for 2025-26 next to the Budget Estimates for 2026-27.

tax-expenditure.definition: The revenue impact of tax incentives such as special rates, exemptions, deductions, rebates, deferrals and credits. The Government describes it as an indirect subsidy to preferred taxpayers. The Union Budget reports it each year in the Statement of Revenue Impact of Tax Incentives under the Central Tax System, which until 2014-15 was called the Statement of Revenue Forgone. The estimates show the potential revenue gain from removing each incentive, assuming the tax base does not change.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Receipt Budget 2026-27, Statement of Revenue Impact of Tax Incentives under the Central Tax System (2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/rec/allrec.pdf
tax-expenditure.example: The Receipt Budget 2026-27 estimates that the deduction for profits of cooperative societies accounts for 71.26 per cent of the total revenue impact of tax incentives for firms, associations of persons and bodies of individuals in 2023-24.

vertical-devolution.definition: The share of the net proceeds of Union taxes (the divisible pool) that is passed to the states collectively on the recommendation of the Finance Commission. The 15th Finance Commission set it at 41 per cent, and the 16th Finance Commission recommended keeping it at 41 per cent for 2026-31, which the Government accepted.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Explanatory Memorandum as to the Action Taken on the Recommendations Made by the Sixteenth Finance Commission (February 2026). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/16fc.pdf
vertical-devolution.example: If the divisible pool in a year is 100 rupees, 41 rupees go to the states as a group and are then shared among them by the horizontal devolution formula.

planning-commission.definition: The body set up on 15 March 1950 by a Cabinet Resolution of the Government of India, which prepared the country's Five Year Plans. It had no basis in the Constitution or in a statute. A Cabinet Resolution of 1 January 2015 created NITI Aayog and superseded the 1950 resolution from that date.
sources: Cabinet Secretariat, Government of India, Resolution No. 511/2/1/2015-Cab. constituting NITI Aayog, Gazette of India Extraordinary (1 January 2015). https://www.niti.gov.in/sites/default/files/2018-12/cabinet-resolution_EN.pdf
planning-commission.example: NITI Aayog was set up by a Cabinet Resolution dated 1 January 2015, which superseded Resolution No. 1-P(C)/50 of 15 March 1950 that had created the Planning Commission.

sdg-india-index.definition: NITI Aayog's index of progress by States and Union Territories on the Sustainable Development Goals. The 2023-24 edition, the fourth since 2018, tracks 113 indicators aligned to MoSPI's National Indicator Framework, gives goal-wise scores on 16 SDGs, and averages them into a composite score. Goal 14 is left out of the composite because it applies only to the nine coastal states.
sources: Press Information Bureau, Release of SDG India Index 2023-24 (12 July 2024). https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2032857&reg=48&lang=2
sdg-india-index.example: In the 2023-24 edition the composite scores of states ranged from 57 to 79, compared with 42 to 69 in 2018.

public-good.definition: A good that is both non-excludable (no one can be prevented from consuming it) and non-rival (one person's use does not reduce what is available to others). Because people can benefit without paying, they have an incentive to free ride, and free markets can be expected to supply too little of such goods.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Julian Reiss, Public Goods (2021). https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/public-goods/
public-good.example: National defence and lighthouses are standard examples. Ships that benefit from a lighthouse cannot be made to pay for it.

public-goods.definition: Goods that are non-excludable (cannot prevent access) and non-rivalrous (one person's use doesn't reduce availability), typically underprovided by markets.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Julian Reiss, Public Goods (2021). https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/public-goods/
public-goods.example: National defence, street lighting and basic research are common examples, and markets tend to supply too little of them without public provision or support.

satisficing.definition: Herbert Simon's term for decision-making that seeks a 'good enough' solution given bounded rationality, rather than the theoretically optimal one.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Bounded Rationality (2018, revised 2024). https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/bounded-rationality/
satisficing.example: An officer who approves the first worksite proposal that meets the minimum criteria, without comparing every proposal, is satisficing.

rule-of-law.definition: A principle of governance in which all persons, institutions and entities, public and private, including the State itself, are accountable to laws that are publicly promulgated, equally enforced and independently adjudicated, and which are consistent with international human rights norms and standards.
sources: United Nations, What is the Rule of Law (United Nations and the Rule of Law). https://www.un.org/ruleoflaw/what-is-the-rule-of-law/
rule-of-law.example: When a minister and a private citizen are bound by the same laws and can be held to account before the same independent courts, the rule of law is being upheld.

transfer-problem.definition: The use of frequent transfers of civil servants as an instrument of political control. Iyer and Mani (2012) show, using career data on Indian Administrative Service officers, that politicians use reassignments across posts of varying importance to control bureaucrats, that political turnover leads to more transfers, and that officers of higher ability face fewer political transfers.
sources: Lakshmi Iyer and Anandi Mani, Traveling Agents: Political Change and Bureaucratic Turnover in India, Review of Economics and Statistics 94(3) (2012), authors' final version. https://sites.nd.edu/lakshmi-iyer/files/2022/03/Iyer_Mani_Bureaucrats_REStatFinalVersion.pdf
transfer-problem.example: Iyer and Mani found no significant difference in immunisation coverage or road completion between districts with more and fewer politically induced transfers. They found somewhat slower long-run poverty reduction where such transfers were more likely, and treated that result as suggestive only.

voice.definition: In Appadurai's framework, which draws on Hirschman, the capacity of the poor to debate, contest, inquire and participate critically, and so to express their views and get results that serve their own welfare. Appadurai treats voice as a cultural capacity that must work through norms and performances with local force, and argues that it and the capacity to aspire strengthen each other. He sees the lack of resources to exercise voice as one of the gravest lacks of the poor.
sources: Arjun Appadurai, The Capacity to Aspire: Culture and the Terms of Recognition, in Rao and Walton (eds), Culture and Public Action, Stanford University Press (2004).

terms-of-recognition.definition: Appadurai's term, by analogy with the terms of trade, for the conditions and constraints under which the poor negotiate with the norms that frame their social lives. He argues that poverty is partly a matter of very weak terms of recognition, where the poor are encouraged to accept norms that further reduce their dignity and access to goods and services, and that strengthening their voice is the way to change these terms.
sources: Arjun Appadurai, The Capacity to Aspire: Culture and the Terms of Recognition, in Rao and Walton (eds), Culture and Public Action, Stanford University Press (2004).

outliers.definition: Observations that lie an abnormal distance from the other values in a sample. An outlier may be a recording or measurement error, or a real value that carries useful information about the process being studied, so it should be investigated before it is removed. In a chart, an extreme value can also stretch the scale and squeeze the other points together.
sources: NIST/SEMATECH, e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, What are outliers in the data? https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section1/prc16.htm
outliers.example: A district reporting an average household size of 40 is probably a data entry error and should be checked against the source records.

q-q-plot.definition: A chart comparing two probability distributions by plotting their quantiles against each other.
sources: NIST/SEMATECH, e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Quantile-Quantile Plot. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/qqplot.htm
q-q-plot.example: A Q-Q plot of a sample against the normal distribution shows whether the data are roughly normal. If they are, the points lie close to a straight line.

scatter-plot.definition: A chart using Cartesian coordinates to display values for two variables, with each point representing an observation.
sources: NIST/SEMATECH, e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Scatter Plot. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/scatterp.htm
scatter-plot.example: Plotting GDP per capita against life expectancy, with one point per country, shows how the two are related.

precision.definition: The level of exactness in measurement, how narrowly clustered repeated measurements are around their central value.
sources: NIST, Special Publication 260-136, Metrological Tools for the Reference Materials and Reference Instruments of the NIST Material Measurement Laboratory, Precision (2021). https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.260-136-2021.pdf
precision.example: A survey with ±15% confidence interval is less precise than one with ±5%, both might be accurate but the first is imprecise.

power-calculation.definition: A calculation of the sample size needed to detect a given minimum detectable effect, or of the smallest effect detectable with a given sample. It depends on the chosen significance level, the desired power, the variance of the outcome, the share of units assigned to treatment and, for clustered designs, the intra-cluster correlation. Power is usually set at 80 per cent and significance at 5 per cent.
sources: J-PAL, Sabhya Gupta and Sarah Kopper, Power calculations, Research Resources (updated August 2021). https://www.povertyactionlab.org/resource/power-calculations
World Bank, Gertler et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, Second Edition, Glossary (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
power-calculation.example: A power calculation tells a team how many children each arm needs for an 80 per cent chance of detecting a 10 percentage point fall in stunting at the 5 per cent significance level, given the baseline stunting rate.

statistical-significance.definition: A result is called statistically significant when its p-value is below a threshold chosen in advance, usually 0.05 (the significance level). The significance level is the accepted risk of a type I error, that is, of finding an impact that does not exist. A p-value indicates how incompatible the data are with a specified model, usually one of no effect. It is not the probability that the result is due to chance or that the hypothesis is true, and it does not measure the size or importance of an effect.
sources: American Statistical Association, ASA Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values, press release (7 March 2016). https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf
World Bank, Gertler et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, Second Edition, Glossary (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
statistical-significance.example: A 12 per cent increase with p = 0.02 is statistically significant at the 5 per cent level. This does not mean there is only a 2 per cent chance the difference arose randomly, and it says nothing about whether 12 per cent is a large effect.

regression-discontinuity.definition: A method exploiting arbitrary cutoffs in program eligibility to estimate causal effects by comparing units just above and below the threshold.
sources: World Bank, Gertler et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, Second Edition, Glossary (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
J-PAL, Michael Gibson and Anja Sautmann, Introduction to randomized evaluations (updated April 2023). https://www.povertyactionlab.org/resource/introduction-evaluations
regression-discontinuity.example: Households just below the BPL cutoff (who received benefits) were compared to those just above (who didn't) to estimate program impact.

quasi-experimental-design.definition: Non-randomized designs that construct comparison groups through statistical methods like matching, difference-in-differences, or regression discontinuity.
sources: World Bank, Gertler et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, Second Edition, Glossary (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
quasi-experimental-design.example: A DiD study compared changes in districts that received the program to similar districts that didn't, controlling for pre-existing differences.

treatment-effect.definition: The causal effect of an intervention on an outcome, meaning the change in outcomes that can be attributed to it. The average treatment effect (ATE) is the average impact across the units in an evaluation when all units assigned to the programme take it up and no comparison units do. When take-up is partial, the treatment-on-the-treated (TOT) estimate measures the effect for the units that actually received it.
sources: World Bank, Gertler et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, Second Edition, Glossary (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
treatment-effect.example: The average increase in consumption caused by receiving the cash transfer.

sampling-frame.definition: The complete list of units from which a sample is drawn, defining the population the sample represents.
sources: World Bank, Gertler et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, Second Edition, Glossary (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
sampling-frame.example: If a village household register is used as the sampling frame, households missing from the register have no chance of being selected, which creates coverage bias.

smart-indicators.definition: An acronym for the qualities of a good indicator. The letters are expanded in different ways. The World Bank's Impact Evaluation in Practice uses specific, measurable, attributable, realistic and targeted, while other guides use achievable, relevant and time-bound for the last three letters.
sources: World Bank, Gertler et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, Second Edition, Glossary (2016). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/25030
smart-indicators.example: '% of target households with access to improved water sources within 500m by December 2025' is SMART; 'improved water access' is not.

regression.definition: Predicting a continuous numerical value rather than a category.
sources: scikit-learn 1.4 documentation, An introduction to machine learning with scikit-learn. https://scikit-learn.org/1.4/tutorial/basic/tutorial.html
regression.example: Predicting household income or consumption expenditure from survey variables.

supervised-learning.definition: Machine learning in which the model learns from labelled examples (pairs of inputs and the outputs to be predicted), so that it can predict the output for new inputs. Classification and regression are the two main kinds.
sources: scikit-learn 1.4 documentation, An introduction to machine learning with scikit-learn. https://scikit-learn.org/1.4/tutorial/basic/tutorial.html
supervised-learning.example: Training a model on households labeled 'poor' or 'non-poor' to predict poverty status.

unsupervised-learning.definition: ML where the model finds patterns in unlabeled data. Useful for exploration and clustering.
sources: scikit-learn 1.4 documentation, An introduction to machine learning with scikit-learn. https://scikit-learn.org/1.4/tutorial/basic/tutorial.html
unsupervised-learning.example: Clustering beneficiaries into groups based on similar characteristics without predefined categories.

training-data.definition: The dataset used to teach an ML model patterns. Model quality depends heavily on training data quality and representativeness.
sources: scikit-learn 1.4 documentation, An introduction to machine learning with scikit-learn. https://scikit-learn.org/1.4/tutorial/basic/tutorial.html
training-data.example: Historical poverty survey data used to train a poverty prediction model.

random-forest.definition: An ensemble machine learning method that builds many decision trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the training data and with a random subset of features considered at each split, and combines their predictions by voting or averaging. Combining many trees reduces the variance and overfitting of single trees. A forest is harder to read than a single tree, and its feature importance scores can mislead.
sources: scikit-learn 1.4 documentation, Ensembles: random forests (citing Breiman, Random Forests, Machine Learning 45(1), 2001). https://scikit-learn.org/1.4/modules/ensemble.html
random-forest.example: A random forest model for PMT-style poverty targeting.

overfitting.definition: When a model learns the training data too well, including noise, and fails to generalize to new data.
sources: scikit-learn 1.4 documentation, Underfitting vs. Overfitting. https://scikit-learn.org/1.4/auto_examples/model_selection/plot_underfitting_overfitting.html
overfitting.example: A model that perfectly predicts poverty in the training district but fails in other districts.

tokenization.definition: Breaking text into smaller units (tokens) like words or subwords. The first step in most NLP pipelines.
sources: Manning, Raghavan and Schutze, Introduction to Information Retrieval, Cambridge University Press (2008), Tokenization. https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/tokenization-1.html
tokenization.example: Splitting 'food security' into tokens ['food', 'security'] for analysis.

sentiment-analysis.definition: Classifying the sentiment of a text, that is, the positive or negative orientation that the writer expresses towards something. Many applications also use a neutral class.
sources: Daniel Jurafsky and James H. Martin, Speech and Language Processing, 3rd edition draft, Chapter 4 Logistic Regression and Text Classification (2026). https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/4.pdf
sentiment-analysis.example: Classifying beneficiary feedback messages as satisfied or dissatisfied.

topic-modeling.definition: Discovering abstract topics in a collection of documents. Useful for exploring large text datasets.
sources: David M. Blei, Probabilistic Topic Models, Communications of the ACM 55(4) (2012). https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~blei/papers/Blei2012.pdf
topic-modeling.example: Finding that beneficiary complaints cluster around 'delays', 'staff behavior', and 'eligibility'.

transfer-learning.definition: Using a model trained on one task as the starting point for a different but related task. Reduces data requirements.
sources: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning, section 14.2 Fine-Tuning. https://d2l.ai/chapter_computer-vision/fine-tuning.html
transfer-learning.example: Using a model trained on ImageNet to extract features from satellite images for poverty prediction.

sparklines.definition: Edward Tufte's term for small, data-intense, design-simple, word-sized graphics that can be embedded in a sentence, table, headline or map. They usually leave out axes and rely on the surrounding text and layout for context.
sources: Edward Tufte, Sparkline theory and practice. https://www.edwardtufte.com/notebook/sparkline-theory-and-practice-edward-tufte/
sparklines.example: Embedding tiny line charts next to each country's name in a table shows GDP trends at a glance.

treemap.definition: A visualization displaying hierarchical data as nested rectangles, where size represents a quantitative variable.
sources: Ben Shneiderman, Human-Computer Interaction Lab, University of Maryland, Treemaps for space-constrained visualization of hierarchies. https://www.cs.umd.edu/hcil/treemap-history/
treemap.example: Showing government budget allocation where rectangle size indicates spending amount for each department.

pre-attentive-attributes.definition: Visual properties that viewers can detect in a large display in less than about 200 to 250 milliseconds, before focused attention, such as hue, size, orientation, length, curvature and motion. The time threshold is a typical figure, and attention still plays some part at this stage.
sources: Christopher G. Healey, Perception in Visualization, North Carolina State University. https://www.csc2.ncsu.edu/faculty/healey/PP/
pre-attentive-attributes.example: A single red dot among blue dots 'pops out' instantly due to pre-attentive color processing.

svg.definition: An XML-based vector image format for two-dimensional graphics that scales without losing quality.
sources: W3C, Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) 2, Chapter 1 Introduction. https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG2/intro.html
svg.example: Charts exported as SVG remain crisp at any size, unlike pixel-based formats like PNG.

semantic-html.definition: Using meaningful HTML elements (headings, lists, tables) that convey structure to assistive technologies.
sources: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, WCAG 2.2 Technique H51: Using table markup to present tabular information. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/html/H51
semantic-html.example: Using <table> for data tables rather than <div> elements helps screen readers navigate.

resolution.definition: For satellite and other georeferenced data, spatial resolution is the smallest horizontal distance between successive elements of data, in practice the ground size of one pixel. Finer resolution shows smaller features.
sources: NASA Earthdata, Remote Sensing (Earth Observation Data Basics). https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/learn/earth-observation-data-basics/remote-sensing
resolution.example: At 10 metre resolution each pixel covers 10 m by 10 m on the ground, which is enough to see large fields but not individual houses.

satellite-imagery.definition: Images captured by satellites orbiting Earth. Key data source for remote monitoring in development.
sources: NASA Earthdata, Remote Sensing (Earth Observation Data Basics). https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/learn/earth-observation-data-basics/remote-sensing
satellite-imagery.example: Sentinel-2 imagery for agricultural monitoring; nighttime lights for economic activity.

technical-debt.definition: Accumulated cost of quick fixes and shortcuts in technology systems. Grows over time if not addressed.
sources: Ward Cunningham, The WyCash Portfolio Management System, OOPSLA '92 Experience Report (1992). http://c2.com/doc/oopsla92.html
technical-debt.example: Manual data cleaning workarounds that become unsustainable as data volume grows.

privacy.definition: An interest in, or right to, control over information about oneself. In the influential account of Alan Westin, it is the ability of people to determine for themselves when, how and to what extent information about them is communicated to others. Other accounts stress limits on access to a person or the appropriate flow of information. AI systems can threaten privacy by building profiles and drawing inferences from data that people did not knowingly share.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Privacy (2002, revised 2023). https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/privacy/
privacy.example: Even without names, combining location + demographics can re-identify individuals.

property-rights.definition: Recognised claims over a resource, usually understood as a bundle of rights that can vary from case to case. The right to exclude others is generally seen as central. The bundle typically also includes the liberty to use the resource, the power to let others use it, and the power to transfer it by gift, sale or inheritance.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Property and Ownership (2004, revised 2026). https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/property/
property-rights.example: A household that holds clear, recorded title to its land can lease it out or sell it.

poverty-gap.definition: The poverty gap index adds up how far each poor person falls below the poverty line, counts the gap as zero for everyone who is not poor, averages it over the whole population, and expresses the result as a percentage of the poverty line. It reflects the depth of poverty as well as its incidence.
sources: World Bank, Poverty and Inequality Platform Methodology Handbook, Calculating survey estimates of poverty and inequality. https://datanalytics.worldbank.org/PIP-Methodology/surveyestimates.html
poverty-gap.example: Dividing the poverty gap index by the headcount ratio gives the average shortfall of the poor themselves, as a share of the poverty line. A poverty gap index of 5 per cent with a headcount of 25 per cent means the poor fall short of the line by 20 per cent on average.

relative-poverty.definition: Poverty measured against the living standards of the society in which a person lives, so that the line rises as typical incomes rise. The European Union's at-risk-of-poverty threshold is 60 per cent of national median equivalised disposable income after social transfers. Eurostat notes that this indicator measures low income compared with other residents and does not measure wealth or poverty as such. The World Bank's societal poverty line is the higher of the international poverty line ($3.00 a day) and $1.30 plus half of the country's median consumption.
sources: Eurostat, Glossary: At-risk-of-poverty rate. https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate
World Bank, Poverty and Inequality Platform Methodology Handbook, Calculating survey estimates of poverty and inequality. https://datanalytics.worldbank.org/PIP-Methodology/surveyestimates.html
relative-poverty.example: Two households with the same income may count as relatively poor in a richer country and not in a poorer one, because each country's line depends on its own median.

poverty-trap.definition: A self-reinforcing mechanism where poverty persists because the poor lack the resources to escape it, low income leads to low savings, low investment, and continued low income.
sources: Aart Kraay and David McKenzie, Do Poverty Traps Exist? Assessing the Evidence, Journal of Economic Perspectives 28(3) (2014). https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.28.3.127
poverty-trap.example: A farmer too poor to afford fertiliser produces less, earns less and stays unable to afford fertiliser, which would be a poverty trap if it holds. Kraay and McKenzie's review finds such traps rare in the evidence and most likely in remote or otherwise disadvantaged areas.

solow-growth-model.definition: A neoclassical model showing that long-run economic growth depends on technological progress, with capital accumulation subject to diminishing returns.
sources: Nobel Prize Outreach, The Prize in Economic Sciences 1987, press release (Robert M. Solow). https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1987/press-release/
solow-growth-model.example: The model explains why simply adding more machines (capital) eventually yields smaller growth gains without technological innovation.

regulatory-capture.definition: George Stigler's argument that regulation can serve the interests of the industries and occupational groups it regulates, protecting producers instead of the general public it was meant to protect. On this view regulation is itself an outcome of the optimising behaviour of market participants.
sources: Nobel Prize Outreach, The Prize in Economic Sciences 1982, press release (George J. Stigler). https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1982/press-release/
regulatory-capture.example: A licensing rule that is presented as protecting consumers but mainly keeps new competitors out of a profession fits Stigler's account.

principal-agent-problem.definition: A situation in which a principal relies on an agent to act on its behalf, their interests differ, and the principal cannot fully observe what the agent does. Contract theory studies how to design pay and other terms so that the agent's rewards are linked to information about performance, weighing incentives against risk. In government, the principal may be a ministry or citizens and the agent a civil servant, contractor or frontline worker.
sources: Nobel Prize Outreach, The Prize in Economic Sciences 2016, press release (Oliver Hart and Bengt Holmstrom, contract theory). https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2016/press-release/
principal-agent-problem.example: PDS dealers diverting subsidised grain are agents whose private interests (profit from diversion) conflict with their principal's (government's) objective of beneficiary delivery.

returns-to-education.definition: The gain from an investment in education, usually measured as the percentage increase in earnings from one more year of schooling. Private returns compare the earnings gain with the costs borne by the individual. Social returns also count the public cost of education; as usually estimated they are lower than private returns because they include public subsidies but leave out wider social benefits.
sources: World Bank, George Psacharopoulos and Harry Anthony Patrinos, Returns to Investment in Education: A Decennial Review of the Global Literature, Policy Research Working Paper 8402 (2018). https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/442521523465644318/pdf/WPS8402.pdf
returns-to-education.example: A World Bank review of 1,120 estimates in 139 countries puts the average private return to an extra year of schooling at about 9 per cent a year. Social returns fall with the level of education, while private returns to higher education have risen and remain high.

resource-curse.definition: The observation that countries with oil or other natural resource wealth have often failed to grow faster than countries without it. Suggested channels include long-term trends and volatility in commodity prices, crowding out of manufacturing, civil war, poor institutions and Dutch disease. The idea is contested, since some commodity exporters have done well and resource wealth is not independent of other conditions.
sources: Jeffrey A. Frankel, The Natural Resource Curse: A Survey, NBER Working Paper 15836 (2010). https://www.nber.org/papers/w15836
resource-curse.example: Policies countries have tried in order to avoid the curse include Chile-style fiscal rules, transparent commodity funds and hedging of export earnings.

street-level-bureaucracy.definition: Michael Lipsky's term for public service workers who deal directly with the public, such as teachers, police officers, social workers and legal-aid lawyers. Because they use considerable discretion in carrying out programmes day to day, they in effect act as policy makers.
sources: Russell Sage Foundation, Michael Lipsky, Street-Level Bureaucracy: Dilemmas of the Individual in Public Services, 30th Anniversary Expanded Edition (2010; first published 1980). https://www.russellsage.org/publications/street-level-bureaucracy
street-level-bureaucracy.example: An ASHA worker deciding which households to prioritise for immunisation follow-up is making a policy decision as well as executing orders.

savings-constraints.definition: Barriers to saving including lack of access to safe savings products, social pressure to share, present-biased preferences, and transaction costs.
sources: J-PAL, Commitment Savings Products in the Philippines (Nava Ashraf, Dean Karlan, Wes Yin). https://www.povertyactionlab.org/evaluation/commitment-savings-products-philippines
savings-constraints.example: In a trial in the Philippines by Ashraf, Karlan and Yin, a commitment savings account that restricted withdrawals was taken up by 28 per cent of clients offered it, and average savings balances in the group offered it rose by 82 per cent after a year.

regression-line.definition: A line fitted to scatter plot data showing the predicted relationship between variables.
sources: NIST/SEMATECH, e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Linear Least Squares Regression. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pmd/section1/pmd141.htm
regression-line.example: Adding a least-squares line to a scatter plot of household income against food spending shows the average relationship between the two.

timeliness.definition: In data quality, the time between the end of the period the data refer to and the release of the data. Data that arrive late are less useful for decisions, however accurate they are.
sources: Eurostat, Glossary: Timeliness. https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Timeliness
timeliness.example: Baseline data arriving 6 months after program start cannot inform initial targeting or design decisions.

outcome-mapping.definition: An approach to planning, monitoring and evaluation developed at IDRC that focuses on outcomes defined as changes in the behaviour, relationships, actions and activities of boundary partners, the people, groups and organisations a programme works with directly. It moves away from assessing a programme's products, because development impacts result from many actors and no single agency can claim full credit.
sources: IDRC, Sarah Earl, Fred Carden and Terry Smutylo, Outcome Mapping: Building Learning and Reflection into Development Programs (2001). https://idrc-crdi.ca/en/book/outcome-mapping-building-learning-and-reflection-development-programs
outcome-mapping.example: Instead of measuring farmer income (hard to attribute), outcome mapping tracks changes in how extension workers engage with farmers.

terms-of-trade.definition: The ratio of export prices to import prices, improvements mean a country can buy more imports for a given amount of exports.
sources: World Bank, World Development Indicators, Net barter terms of trade index (2015 = 100), TT.PRI.MRCH.XD.WD, indicator metadata (source: UNCTAD). https://api.worldbank.org/v2/indicator/TT.PRI.MRCH.XD.WD?format=json
terms-of-trade.example: Commodity exporters face volatile terms of trade; coffee price drops mean more bags must be sold to buy the same tractor.

rights-based-approach.definition: An approach to development that is based on international human rights standards and directed at promoting and protecting human rights. It identifies rights-holders and their entitlements and the corresponding duty-bearers and their obligations, and works to strengthen the capacity of rights-holders to make claims and of duty-bearers to meet them. In Indian social policy the term is also used for laws that make welfare entitlements legally enforceable, so that people can claim them and officials can be held to account.
sources: Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Frequently Asked Questions on a Human Rights-Based Approach to Development Cooperation (2006). https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/Publications/FAQen.pdf

India Code, The Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (Act No. 36 of 2025), section 11. https://indiacode.gov.in/items/63b87434-40a1-4eaf-a44e-adcc29215670
rights-based-approach.example: Under the rural employment guarantee, an applicant who is not given work within fifteen days is legally entitled to an unemployment allowance.

webers-law.definition: The principle that the just-noticeable difference between stimuli is proportional to their magnitude.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Weber's law (2020). https://www.britannica.com/science/Webers-law
webers-law.example: Distinguishing between bars of 100 and 105 pixels is harder than between 10 and 15 pixels.

worksite-facility.definition: The minimum amenities that India's rural employment guarantee law requires at every worksite. Workers must have safe drinking water, shade for children and periods of rest, and a first-aid box for minor injuries. Where five or more children under the age of five accompany the women working at a site, one of the women is deputed to look after them and is paid the wage rate. These provisions sat in Schedule II of MGNREGA and are carried into Schedule II of the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, which came into force on 1 July 2026.
sources: Government of India, The Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (Act 36 of 2025), Schedule II and section 37. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/bills_parliament/2025/Viksit_Bharat_G_RAM_G_Act_2025.pdf
PRS Legislative Research, The VB-G RAM G Bill, 2025 (2025). https://prsindia.org/billtrack/the-viksit-bharat-%E2%80%93-guarantee-for-rozgar-and-ajeevika-mission-gramin-vb-%E2%80%93-g-ram-g-bill-2025
worksite-facility.example: A Gram Panchayat opening a pond-desilting work arranges drinking water, a shaded rest area and a first-aid box at the site, and pays one woman worker to care for the young children who come with their mothers.

world-bank-ieg.definition: The Independent Evaluation Group (IEG) evaluates the development effectiveness of the World Bank Group. It is independent of World Bank management and reports directly to the Board of Executive Directors, and its work aims to draw lessons from past experience and to hold the institution accountable to shareholders and stakeholders.
sources: World Bank Group, Independent Evaluation Group, About IEG. https://ieg.worldbankgroup.org/about-us
world-bank-ieg.example: A team preparing a new World Bank project in rural water supply can read IEG's evaluations of earlier projects in the sector for lessons on what went wrong before.

developmental-evaluation.definition: An evaluation approach designed for programs operating in complex, fast-changing conditions where goals and strategies are still emerging. The evaluator works alongside the team in real time, feeding back data to support adaptation rather than judging a fixed model against fixed targets. Use it for innovation, systems-change or pilot work where a conventional summative design would freeze something that is meant to keep evolving.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, second edition (2023). https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
developmental-evaluation.example: A livelihoods incubator testing a new farmer-collective model could use developmental evaluation, with the evaluator joining weekly design meetings and feeding back data as the model changes.

outcome-harvesting.definition: A method that works backwards from observed changes ('outcomes') to determine whether and how an intervention contributed to them, rather than measuring progress against pre-set indicators. Harvesters collect specific, verifiable statements of who changed what, then substantiate them with independent sources. Use it for advocacy, network or governance work where results are unpredictable and hard to define in advance.
sources: Wilson-Grau, R. and Britt, H., Outcome Harvesting, Ford Foundation MENA Office (2012, revised 2013). https://cnxus.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/wilsongrau_en_Outome20Harvesting20Brief_revised20Nov202013.pdf
outcome-harvesting.example: A coalition working on forest-rights advocacy could use outcome harvesting to record unexpected results, such as an official issuing new titles, that no logframe indicator had anticipated, and then check each one with independent informants.

process-tracing.definition: A within-case method that tests causal claims by examining the specific evidence a hypothesis should leave behind if it were true. Analysts apply tests such as 'hoop' (necessary evidence) and 'smoking gun' (sufficient evidence) to update confidence in competing explanations. Use it in single cases or small-n evaluations to establish causal mechanisms rather than statistical association.
sources: Collier, D., Understanding Process Tracing, PS: Political Science and Politics 44(4) (2011). https://polisci.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/people/u3827/Understanding%20Process%20Tracing.pdf
process-tracing.example: To learn why one district's sanitation drive succeeded while a neighbour's failed, an evaluator could use process tracing to test whether frontline-worker incentives, rather than funding alone, were the decisive mechanism.

realist-evaluation.definition: A theory-driven approach that asks not simply 'does it work?' but 'what works, for whom, in what circumstances, and why?'. It is organised around context-mechanism-outcome (CMO) configurations, explaining how a program's resources trigger participants' reasoning to produce results in particular settings. Use it when the same intervention produces different results across sites and you need to explain that variation.
sources: UK Government (Office for Health Improvement and Disparities), A brief introduction to realist evaluation (2021). https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1004663/Brief_introduction_to_realist_evaluation.pdf
realist-evaluation.example: A realist evaluation of a cash transfer run in several states would ask why it raised school attendance in some places and not others, testing ideas such as whether nearby banking access changed how families responded.

regression-discontinuity-design.definition: A quasi-experimental method used when eligibility for a program is decided by a cutoff on a continuous score, such as an income line or test mark. Because people just above and just below the threshold are otherwise very similar, comparing them yields a near-experimental estimate of impact around the cutoff. Use it wherever a sharp administrative rule assigns treatment.
sources: Gertler, P. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, World Bank (2011), Glossary. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/823791468325239704/pdf/Impact-evaluation-in-practice.pdf
regression-discontinuity-design.example: An evaluation of a scholarship awarded to students scoring above a fixed exam mark used regression discontinuity, comparing college enrolment for applicants just above versus just below the cutoff.

qualitative-data-saturation.definition: The point in qualitative data collection or analysis at which new interviews or observations stop yielding new themes, codes or insights, so that further data would mostly repeat what is already known. It is widely used as a rule for deciding when to stop collecting data and is often cited to justify the size of a qualitative sample. Methodologists caution that it is a judgement about data not yet collected, that it is better treated as a matter of degree, and that a study should say how it was assessed.
sources: Saunders, B. et al., Saturation in qualitative research: exploring its conceptualization and operationalization, Quality and Quantity 52 (2018). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5993836/
qualitative-data-saturation.example: After 18 farmer interviews on a crop-insurance rollout, the researchers reached saturation when three successive conversations surfaced no new barriers, and stopped adding respondents.

benchmarking.definition: The practice of comparing a program's performance against a reference point such as a peer program, an industry standard, a prior period or a national average, to judge whether results are strong or weak. It turns an abstract number into a meaningful one by giving it context. Use it when stakeholders ask 'is this good?' and you need a defensible standard of comparison.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, second edition (2023), Benchmark. https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
benchmarking.example: An NGO can benchmark the attendance rate in its schools against the district average from official school statistics to show whether its schools are doing better than the local norm.

utilization-focused-evaluation.definition: An evaluation framework built around the principle that evaluations should be judged by how much their intended users actually use them. From the outset, the evaluator identifies primary intended users and designs every choice, including questions, methods and reporting, to fit their real decisions. Use it whenever the risk is that a technically sound report will sit unread on a shelf.
sources: Patton, M. Q., Utilization-Focused Evaluation (U-FE) Checklist, Western Michigan University Evaluation Center (2013). https://wmich.edu/sites/default/files/attachments/u350/2014/UFE_checklist_2013.pdf
utilization-focused-evaluation.example: Before a utilization-focused evaluation of a state health programme begins, the evaluator meets the programme managers who will use it to agree which decisions the findings must inform, and designs the survey around those decisions.

evaluation-rubrics.definition: Explicit, agreed statements that define what different levels of performance (for example poor, adequate, good, excellent) actually look like on each evaluation criterion. Rubrics make evaluative judgements transparent and consistent by settling the standards before the evidence is weighed. Use them to move from describing results to defensibly judging their quality or value.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, second edition (2023), Rubric. https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
evaluation-rubrics.example: An evaluation team co-developed rubrics with a foundation so that 'good community participation' had a shared, written definition rather than being left to each reviewer's instinct.

evaluability-assessment.definition: A structured pre-evaluation check of whether a program is ready to be evaluated in a way that is credible and useful. It examines whether objectives are clear, the theory of change is plausible, data exist, and stakeholders agree on purpose, then recommends whether, when and how to proceed. Use it before commissioning a full evaluation to avoid wasting money on a study that cannot succeed.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, second edition (2023), Evaluability. https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
evaluability-assessment.example: An evaluability assessment of a new watershed program found its outcome targets were undefined and no baseline existed, so the funder invested first in an M&E system before commissioning an impact study.

theory-based-evaluation.definition: An umbrella approach that tests a program against its explicit theory of how and why it is expected to work, examining each causal link rather than only measuring end results. It opens the 'black box' between activities and outcomes, explaining why an effect did or did not occur. Use it in complex programs where knowing the mechanism matters as much as knowing the impact.
sources: White, H., Theory-Based Impact Evaluation: Principles and Practice, 3ie Working Paper 3 (2009). https://www.3ieimpact.org/sites/default/files/2017-11/Working_Paper_3.pdf
theory-based-evaluation.example: A theory-based evaluation of a farmer producer organisation scheme would test each assumed step, from training to collective bargaining to higher prices, to find where the chain holds and where it breaks.

mixed-methods-evaluation.definition: An evaluation design that deliberately integrates quantitative and qualitative approaches to theory, data collection, analysis and interpretation, so that numbers show how much changed while qualitative evidence explains how and why. The two strands can run one after the other or at the same time, and are analysed together. The aim is more reliable data, more valid findings and a better understanding of how context shapes results.
sources: Bamberger, M., Introduction to Mixed Methods in Impact Evaluation, InterAction Impact Evaluation Notes No. 3 (2012). https://www.interaction.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/Mixed-Methods-in-Impact-Evaluation-English.pdf
mixed-methods-evaluation.example: A mixed-methods evaluation of a sanitation program paired a household survey measuring latrine use with ethnographic visits explaining why some new latrines were used for storage.

p-value.definition: A p-value is the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the one found, assuming the null hypothesis of no effect is true. A small p-value (commonly below 0.05) suggests the data are unlikely under the null, which is often taken as evidence against it. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true, nor a measure of effect size, and it should never be read in isolation.
sources: American Statistical Association, Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values (2016). https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf
Gertler, P. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, World Bank (2011), Glossary. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/823791468325239704/pdf/Impact-evaluation-in-practice.pdf
p-value.example: An evaluation of a cash-transfer pilot reports a p-value of 0.03 for the change in school attendance. If the pilot had no effect, a difference at least this large would be expected in about 3 per cent of samples. It does not mean there is a 3 per cent chance the result is due to chance alone.

statistical-power.definition: Statistical power is the probability that a study will detect an effect of a given size when that effect exists. It depends on the sample size, the true effect size, the variability of the data, and the chosen significance threshold. Underpowered studies risk missing real effects, which is why power calculations are done before data collection to set an adequate sample size.
sources: Gertler, P. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, World Bank (2011), Glossary. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/823791468325239704/pdf/Impact-evaluation-in-practice.pdf
statistical-power.example: Before launching a sanitation trial across 60 villages, evaluators run a power calculation and find they need 90 villages to reliably detect a 10-point change in latrine use.

standard-deviation.definition: Standard deviation measures how spread out a set of values is around their mean, expressed in the same units as the data. A small standard deviation means values cluster tightly near the average, while a large one means they are widely dispersed. It is the square root of the variance and is a core input to many other statistics such as standard error and effect size.
sources: NIST/SEMATECH, e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.6 Measures of Scale. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda356.htm
OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e, 2.7 Measures of the Spread of the Data. https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/2-7-measures-of-the-spread-of-the-data
standard-deviation.example: Two villages report the same average household income, but one has a much larger standard deviation, revealing far greater inequality within it.

standard-error.definition: The standard error is the standard deviation of a sample statistic, such as a sample mean, across hypothetical repeated samples. It quantifies how much an estimate would vary from sample to sample and shrinks as sample size grows. Standard errors are used to build confidence intervals and to test hypotheses, distinguishing sampling uncertainty from the raw spread of the data.
sources: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e, 2.7 Measures of the Spread of the Data and 7.1 The Central Limit Theorem for Sample Means. https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/2-7-measures-of-the-spread-of-the-data
standard-error.example: A national employment survey reports a mean daily wage with a small standard error because its sample of 100,000 workers makes the estimate very stable.

confounding.definition: Confounding occurs when a third variable is associated with both the presumed cause and the outcome, distorting the apparent relationship between them. If left unadjusted, a confounder can create a spurious association or mask a real one, leading to wrong conclusions about cause and effect. Analysts control for confounders through study design, stratification, matching, or statistical adjustment.
sources: University of Oxford, Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine, Catalogue of Bias, Confounding. https://catalogofbias.org/biases/confounding/
confounding.example: A study finds villages with more NGO clinics have higher child mortality, but wealth is a confounder: poorer areas attract both more clinics and higher mortality.

selection-bias.definition: Selection bias arises when the individuals included in a study differ systematically from the population of interest, so the sample is not representative. It can enter through non-random sampling, self-selection into a program, or differential dropout, and it skews estimates in ways that more data alone cannot fix.
