Randomization and careful sampling frames are the main defenses against it.
sources: University of Oxford, Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine, Catalogue of Bias, Selection bias. https://catalogofbias.org/biases/selection-bias/
Gertler, P. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, World Bank (2011), Glossary. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/823791468325239704/pdf/Impact-evaluation-in-practice.pdf
selection-bias.example: Evaluating a skills program only among graduates who completed it overstates its impact, because the least-motivated participants who dropped out are excluded.

regression-to-the-mean.definition: Regression to the mean is the tendency for extreme measurements to be followed by ones closer to the average, simply because extreme values often reflect temporary chance factors. It can masquerade as a program effect when interventions are targeted at the worst-performing units, which would improve somewhat even without any action. Comparison groups are needed to separate real effects from this statistical artifact.
sources: Barnett, A. G., van der Pols, J. C. and Dobson, A. J., Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it, International Journal of Epidemiology 34(1) (2005). https://academic.oup.com/ije/article/34/1/215/638499
regression-to-the-mean.example: Districts selected for a remedial-teaching drive because of the lowest test scores improve the next year partly because of regression to the mean as well as the intervention.

correlation-coefficient.definition: A correlation coefficient is a number between -1 and +1 that summarizes the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables. Values near +1 or -1 indicate a strong positive or negative association, while values near 0 indicate little linear relationship. Correlation does not imply causation, and it can miss non-linear patterns entirely.
sources: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e, 12.3 The Regression Equation. https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/12-3-the-regression-equation
correlation-coefficient.example: If district data showed a correlation coefficient of 0.7 between female literacy and immunisation rates, that would be a strong positive linear association, but it would not show that literacy causes higher immunisation.

normal-distribution.definition: The normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution defined by its mean and standard deviation, where most values cluster near the center and taper off equally on both sides. Many statistical methods assume approximate normality, and sample means tend toward it as sample size grows under the central limit theorem. Real-world data such as incomes are often skewed rather than normal, so the assumption should always be checked.
sources: NIST/SEMATECH, e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.6.6.1 Normal Distribution. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3661.htm
normal-distribution.example: Adult heights in a large population survey follow a roughly normal distribution, letting analysts use standard-deviation rules to flag unusually short or tall individuals.

skewness.definition: Skewness measures the asymmetry of a distribution around its centre. Positive or right skew means the right tail of high values is long relative to the left, which usually pulls the mean above the median, while negative or left skew means the tail stretches toward low values. Skewed data can make the mean misleading, so the median is often preferred, and transformations may be applied before analysis.
sources: NIST/SEMATECH, e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.11 Measures of Skewness and Kurtosis. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda35b.htm
skewness.example: Household income in a survey is strongly right-skewed because a few very wealthy households pull the average well above what a typical family earns.

outlier.definition: An outlier is a data point that lies far from the bulk of the observations, whether due to real rare events, measurement error, or data-entry mistakes. Outliers can heavily distort means, variances, and regression results, so they should be investigated rather than automatically deleted. Robust statistics and clear documentation of any exclusions help handle them transparently.
sources: NIST/SEMATECH, e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.17 Detection of Outliers. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda35h.htm
outlier.example: A price-monitoring dataset shows a wheat rate of 9,000 rupees per kilogram, an obvious outlier caused by a decimal-point data-entry error.

imputation.definition: Imputation is the practice of filling in missing values in a dataset with estimated ones so that analyses can proceed without discarding incomplete records. Methods range from simple mean or median substitution to model-based approaches such as multiple imputation that also reflect the uncertainty of the guesses. Poor imputation can bias results, so the missingness mechanism and method should always be reported.
sources: United Nations Statistics Division, Household Sample Surveys in Developing and Transition Countries, Studies in Methods Series F No. 96 (2005), chapter 8. https://unstats.un.org/unsd/hhsurveys/pdf/Household_surveys.pdf
imputation.example: In a panel survey where some households skipped the income question, analysts use multiple imputation drawing on assets and education to estimate the missing values.

weighting.definition: Weighting assigns each observation a multiplier so that a sample better reflects the target population, correcting for unequal selection probabilities and differential non-response. Design weights account for how units were sampled, non-response adjustments correct for units that did not respond, and post-stratification weights align the sample to known population totals such as age or region. Analysing a complex survey without its weights gives biased estimates, and ignoring its stratification and clustering understates standard errors.
sources: United Nations Statistics Division, Designing Household Survey Samples: Practical Guidelines, Studies in Methods Series F No. 98 (2005), sections 5.5 and chapter 7. https://unstats.un.org/unsd/demographic/sources/surveys/Handbook23June05.pdf

International Institute for Population Sciences and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), 2019-21: India Report (2021). https://rchiips.org/nfhs/NFHS-5Reports/NFHS-5_INDIA_REPORT.pdf
weighting.example: India's National Family Health Survey reports almost all its tables on the weighted sample, so that areas sampled at different rates count in proportion to their share of the population.

cross-tabulation.definition: A cross-tabulation is a table that shows the joint frequency distribution of two or more categorical variables, with categories of one variable as rows and another as columns. It reveals how the variables relate, such as whether an outcome differs across groups, and is often paired with a chi-square test of association. Cross-tabs are a fast, transparent first step in exploring survey data.
sources: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e, 3.4 Contingency Tables. https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/3-4-contingency-tables
cross-tabulation.example: A cross-tabulation of toilet ownership by household caste category quickly exposes access gaps across social groups in a district survey.

data-lifecycle.definition: The data lifecycle is the sequence of stages that research data typically pass through, from planning and collection to processing and analysis, publishing and sharing, preservation, and reuse. The stages can overlap or be revisited. Treating data management as a lifecycle means documentation, ethics, security and quality are planned for at each stage, so that others can later find, understand and reuse the data.
sources: UK Data Service, Data lifecycle. https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/learning-hub/data-producer-support/foundations-of-research-data-management/data-lifecycle/
data-lifecycle.example: An NGO maps its monitoring data lifecycle so that consent, cleaning, and secure archiving are planned before field teams begin household visits.

metadata.definition: Metadata is descriptive information about a dataset, such as who collected it, when, where and how, what each variable means, the units used, and how the data were processed. Good metadata makes data discoverable, interpretable and reusable long after the original team has moved on, and it should stay with the data when they are archived or shared.
sources: UK Data Service, Data lifecycle. https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/learning-hub/data-producer-support/foundations-of-research-data-management/data-lifecycle/
metadata.example: A district open-data portal attaches metadata to each rainfall file, recording the gauge location, measurement units, and collection dates.

base-rate.definition: The base rate is the underlying frequency of a characteristic or outcome in a population before any additional information is considered. Ignoring it, known as the base-rate fallacy, leads to badly miscalibrated conclusions, especially when interpreting screening or diagnostic tests for rare conditions. Correct interpretation combines the base rate with test accuracy, often via Bayes' theorem.
sources: Tversky, A. and Kahneman, D., Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science 185 (1974), reprinted in Kahneman, Slovic and Tversky (eds), Cambridge University Press (1982). https://assets.cambridge.org/97805212/84141/excerpt/9780521284141_excerpt.pdf
base-rate.example: Because tuberculosis has a low base rate in a screened group, even a fairly accurate test yields many false positives that must be confirmed.

intention-to-treat.definition: An analysis that keeps participants in their originally assigned group regardless of whether they actually received or complied with the intervention, preserving the benefits of randomisation.
sources: Gertler, P. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, World Bank (2011), Glossary. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/823791468325239704/pdf/Impact-evaluation-in-practice.pdf
intention-to-treat.example: Even though some households never attended the sessions, the ITT analysis kept them in the treatment group.

attrition.definition: The loss of participants from a study over time; if it differs between groups it can bias impact estimates.
sources: Gertler, P. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, World Bank (2011), Glossary. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/823791468325239704/pdf/Impact-evaluation-in-practice.pdf
attrition.example: High attrition among migrant workers threatened the validity of the two-year panel study.

spillover-effect.definition: When a programme affects people who were not directly targeted, which can contaminate a comparison group and bias impact estimates.
sources: Gertler, P. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, World Bank (2011), Glossary. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/823791468325239704/pdf/Impact-evaluation-in-practice.pdf
spillover-effect.example: Cash transfers to some households in a village can raise local wages or prices, so that non-recipients nearby are affected too and are no longer a clean comparison group.

recall-bias.definition: Systematic error introduced when respondents inaccurately remember past events, often worse for distant or sensitive events.
sources: University of Oxford, Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine, Catalogue of Bias, Recall bias. https://catalogofbias.org/biases/recall-bias/
recall-bias.example: Asking mothers to recall a year of health expenses introduced recall bias into the survey.

social-desirability-bias.definition: The tendency of respondents to answer in ways they think are socially acceptable rather than truthfully.
sources: Krumpal, I., Determinants of social desirability bias in sensitive surveys: a literature review, Quality and Quantity 47(4) (2013). https://ideas.repec.org/a/spr/qualqt/v47y2013i4p2025-2047.html
social-desirability-bias.example: Households asked directly whether they defecate in the open may under-report the practice because of social desirability bias.

additionality.definition: The extent to which an outcome happened because of an intervention and would not have occurred anyway.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, second edition (2023), Additionality. https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
additionality.example: A donor checking the additionality of a loan asks whether the project would have been financed by private lenders anyway, and whether it reached people or results that would not otherwise have been reached.

panel-data.definition: Data that follows the same units (people, households, firms) repeatedly over time, enabling analysis of change within units.
sources: United Nations Statistics Division, Household Sample Surveys in Developing and Transition Countries, Studies in Methods Series F No. 96 (2005). https://unstats.un.org/unsd/hhsurveys/pdf/Household_surveys.pdf
panel-data.example: The panel dataset tracked the same 2,000 households across three survey rounds.

cluster-randomization.definition: Randomly assigning groups (clusters) such as villages or schools, rather than individuals, to treatment or control.
sources: Gertler, P. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, World Bank (2011), chapter 4 and Glossary. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/823791468325239704/pdf/Impact-evaluation-in-practice.pdf
cluster-randomization.example: Because the programme operated at village level, the trial used cluster randomization by village.

sampling-weight.definition: A value applied to survey responses so that the sample reflects the population, correcting for unequal selection probabilities and non-response.
sources: United Nations Statistics Division, Designing Household Survey Samples: Practical Guidelines, Studies in Methods Series F No. 98 (2005), section 5.5. https://unstats.un.org/unsd/demographic/sources/surveys/Handbook23June05.pdf
sampling-weight.example: Applying sampling weights corrected the over-representation of urban households in the estimates.

opportunity-cost.definition: The value of the next-best alternative forgone when a choice is made. Every decision to use time, money, or resources one way carries the implicit cost of what could have been done instead. It reminds practitioners that a resource has a price even when no cash changes hands.
sources: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, 2.1 How Individuals Make Choices Based on Their Budget Constraint. https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/2-1-how-individuals-make-choices-based-on-their-budget-constraint
opportunity-cost.example: A girl kept home to fetch water in rural Rajasthan bears the opportunity cost of the schooling and future earnings she loses.

marginal-utility.definition: The additional satisfaction a person gains from consuming one more unit of a good or service. It typically diminishes as consumption rises, meaning each extra unit adds less benefit than the last. Applied to income, the same idea suggests that an extra rupee adds more to the well-being of a poor household than of a rich one.
sources: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, 6.1 Consumption Choices. https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/6-1-consumption-choices
marginal-utility.example: An extra kilogram of rice raises the well-being of a food-insecure family in Bihar far more than it would for an affluent urban household.

elasticity.definition: A measure of how much one variable responds to a change in another, usually the percentage change in quantity demanded or supplied for a percentage change in price. Demand is elastic when quantity reacts sharply and inelastic when it barely moves. Understanding elasticity helps predict how consumers and producers respond to taxes, subsidies, and price shifts.
sources: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, 5.1 Price Elasticity of Demand and Price Elasticity of Supply. https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/5-1-price-elasticity-of-demand-and-price-elasticity-of-supply
elasticity.example: If demand for a staple such as onions is inelastic, a sharp rise in its price increases household spending on it without cutting the quantity bought by much.

deadweight-loss.definition: The loss of economic value that occurs when a market is prevented from reaching its efficient outcome, often by a tax, subsidy, price control, or monopoly. It represents gains from trade that vanish entirely rather than transferring from one party to another. Policymakers weigh deadweight loss against the revenue or equity gains a distortion may deliver.
sources: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, 3.5 Demand, Supply, and Efficiency. https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/3-5-demand-supply-and-efficiency
deadweight-loss.example: A price ceiling on kerosene in India can create shortages and black markets, producing a deadweight loss as willing buyers and sellers fail to transact legally.

informal-economy.definition: All economic activities by workers and economic units that, in law or in practice, are not covered or are insufficiently covered by formal arrangements such as registration, taxation, labour law and social security. It excludes illicit activities. Street vendors, home-based workers, domestic workers and unregistered enterprises are typical examples, and workers in it often lack written contracts, social protection and stable income. The ILO estimates that over 60 per cent of the world's workforce works in the informal economy.
sources: International Labour Organization, Transition from the Informal to the Formal Economy Recommendation, 2015 (No. 204), paragraph 2. https://www.un.org/en/ga/second/70/wcms_377774.pdf
International Labour Organization, Informal economy. https://www.ilo.org/topics-and-sectors/informal-economy
informal-economy.example: A domestic worker paid in cash by the households she cleans for, with no written contract, paid leave or pension, works in the informal economy.

multiplier-effect.definition: The process by which an initial injection of spending generates a larger total increase in economic activity as money is re-spent through successive rounds. Each recipient spends part of the new income, creating income for others. The size of the multiplier depends on how much of each rupee is spent rather than saved or lost to imports.
sources: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, Appendix D The Expenditure-Output Model. https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/d-the-expenditure-output-model
multiplier-effect.example: Wages paid under a rural public works programme that are mostly spent in village shops become income for shopkeepers and producers, who spend part of it in turn, so local demand rises by more than the original wage bill.

purchasing-power-parity-2.definition: A method of comparing living standards across countries by adjusting exchange rates so that a basket of goods costs the same everywhere. It corrects for the fact that a dollar buys far more in low-income countries than in high-income ones. PPP figures give a truer picture of real income and poverty than market exchange rates.
sources: International Monetary Fund, Finance and Development, Back to Basics: Purchasing Power Parity. https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/fandd/issues/Series/Back-to-Basics/Purchasing-Power-Parity-PPP
OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, 19.4 Comparing GDP among Countries. https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/19-4-comparing-gdp-among-countries
purchasing-power-parity-2.example: Converting India's income per person at PPP rather than at the market exchange rate gives a much higher figure, because many goods and services, especially non-traded services, cost less in India than in high-income countries.

universal-basic-income.definition: A policy proposal to pay every citizen a regular, unconditional cash sum regardless of income or employment. Advocates argue it guarantees a floor, cuts administrative complexity, and respects recipients' autonomy. Critics question its cost and whether it should replace or supplement existing targeted schemes.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Economic Survey 2016-17, Chapter 9: Universal Basic Income (2017). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/budget2017-2018/es2016-17/echap09.pdf
universal-basic-income.example: India's Economic Survey 2016-17 discussed a quasi-universal basic income reaching 75 per cent of the population, costed at about 4.9 per cent of GDP, and warned that it would be unaffordable if added on top of existing anti-poverty programmes instead of replacing some of them.

subsidy.definition: A financial contribution by a government or public body, such as a grant, loan, tax concession or provision of goods below cost, that confers a benefit by lowering the cost of producing or consuming a good. Subsidies are used to widen access to essentials or support producers, but they can also distort markets, weigh on budgets and benefit groups other than those intended.
sources: World Trade Organization, Subsidies and countervailing measures: overview. https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/scm_e/subs_e.htm
Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Budget at a Glance 2026-27, Expenditure of Major Items. https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/Budget_at_Glance/budget_at_a_glance.pdf
subsidy.example: India's Union Budget 2026-27 provides about Rs 1.71 lakh crore for the fertiliser subsidy, which keeps the price farmers pay for fertiliser below its cost.

crowding-out.definition: The reduction in private spending or investment that can follow an increase in government spending or borrowing. When the state borrows heavily, it may push up interest rates, which reduces business investment and household consumption. How large the effect is depends on conditions, and public investment can sometimes draw private investment in instead, which is called crowding in.
sources: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, 30.6 Practical Problems with Discretionary Fiscal Policy. https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/30-6-practical-problems-with-discretionary-fiscal-policy
crowding-out.example: Heavy government borrowing to finance India's fiscal deficit can crowd out private firms by pushing up the interest rates they face on loans.

social-protection-floor.definition: A social protection floor is a set of nationally defined basic social security guarantees ensuring everyone has access to essential health care and a minimum income across the life cycle. Promoted by the ILO, it typically covers children, working-age people who cannot earn enough, and older persons. It frames social protection as a right and a floor below which no one should fall.
sources: International Labour Organization, Social Protection Floors Recommendation, 2012 (No. 202), paragraphs 2 and 5. https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_norm/---relconf/documents/meetingdocument/wcms_183326.pdf
social-protection-floor.example: A country's free essential health care, child benefits, income support for working-age people who cannot earn enough, and old-age pensions together make up its social protection floor.

overton-window.definition: The range of policy ideas that the public and politicians consider acceptable or mainstream at a given moment. Ideas outside the window are seen as radical or unthinkable. The window can shift and widen over time, usually through slow changes in society's values and norms, and only occasionally because a politician champions an idea from outside it. The model was developed in the mid-1990s by Joseph P. Overton of the Mackinac Center for Public Policy.
sources: Mackinac Center for Public Policy, The Overton Window. https://www.mackinac.org/OvertonWindow
overton-window.example: An advocacy group that wants a policy currently outside the window may first build public support for a milder version, so that the fuller proposal later falls within what politicians see as acceptable.

path-dependency.definition: The idea that decisions made in the past constrain the options available today, even when the original conditions no longer apply. Early choices set off self-reinforcing processes, or increasing returns, so that the timing and sequence of events matter, small or chance events can have large consequences, and a course of action once taken can be very hard to reverse. Reformers must account for this inertia instead of assuming a clean slate.
sources: Pierson, P., Increasing Returns, Path Dependence, and the Study of Politics, American Political Science Review 94(2) (2000), abstract. https://ideas.repec.org/a/cup/apsrev/v94y2000i02p251-267_22.html
path-dependency.example: Once an administrative system is built around a particular set of land records, later procedures, institutions and disputes all come to depend on those records, which makes replacing them slow and contested.

elite-capture.definition: The tendency for the wealthy, powerful or well-connected to divert public resources, programmes or decentralised institutions to their own benefit. It is a persistent risk in community-driven development and local governance, where formal participation can mask control by dominant castes, landlords or political networks. Researchers distinguish capture from elite control, since in some settings leaders from elite groups still direct benefits to the poor. Remedies studied include transparency, mandated quotas for disadvantaged groups, and social audits.
sources: Mansuri, G. and Rao, V., Localizing Development: Does Participation Work?, World Bank Policy Research Report (2013). https://doi.org/10.1596/978-0-8213-8256-1
elite-capture.example: Evidence from Indian village councils, summarised by the World Bank, finds that reserving council seats and presidencies for women and disadvantaged groups tends to shift local decisions toward the interests of those groups.

decentralisation.definition: The transfer of authority, responsibility, resources and accountability from central to lower levels of government or to local bodies. It can be administrative (deconcentration or delegation to local offices), fiscal (revenue and spending powers) or political (elected local government). In practice, functions are often handed down while the centre keeps control through money, laws and regulation, so the extent of real decentralisation depends on what is transferred.
sources: UNDP and German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development, The UNDP Role in Decentralization and Local Governance: A Joint Evaluation (2000). https://erc.undp.org/evaluation/documents/download/5029
Government of India, The Constitution of India (as on 1 May 2024), Article 243G and the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules. https://legislative.gov.in/constitution-of-india/
decentralisation.example: India's 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments of 1992 provided for elected panchayats and municipalities and listed 29 and 18 subjects that state legislatures may devolve to them, leaving each state to decide how much power and money actually moves.

public-expenditure-review.definition: A systematic analysis of how a government allocates and spends public money in a country or sector, assessing whether spending is adequate, sustainable, efficient, effective and equitable, and aligned with policy priorities. It is one of the World Bank's core diagnostic tools. Because budget data say little about whether money reaches the frontline, reviews are often paired with public expenditure tracking surveys that follow funds down to schools or clinics. Findings inform budget reforms and better expenditure management.
sources: World Bank, Education Public Expenditure Review Guidelines (2017), Preface and Technical Note 12. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/155861497609568842/pdf/Education-public-expenditure-review-guidelines.pdf
public-expenditure-review.example: The first public expenditure tracking survey of Uganda's primary schools found that between 1991 and 1995 schools received on average only 13 per cent of the non-wage grants meant for them, with most of the rest captured by local officials.

direct-benefit-transfer.definition: A mode of delivering subsidies and welfare payments directly into beneficiaries' bank accounts rather than through in-kind goods or intermediaries. In India it is built on the JAM trinity of Jan Dhan bank accounts, Aadhaar identity, and mobile phones, and aims to cut leakage, ghost beneficiaries, and diversion. It shifts the delivery challenge from distribution logistics to accurate targeting and last-mile banking access.
sources: Direct Benefit Transfer Mission, Cabinet Secretariat, Government of India, About Us. https://dbtbharat.gov.in/static-page-content/spagecont?id=1
direct-benefit-transfer.example: Under DBT a scholarship is paid straight into the student's bank account instead of through an intermediary, so an eligible student whose account details are wrong or not linked can miss a payment until the record is corrected.

grievance-redressal.definition: The systems and procedures through which citizens can report problems with a public service or entitlement and have them resolved. A grievance is lodged, sent to the department responsible, and tracked until it is settled. Good mechanisms are easy to reach, set time limits, record each case and allow appeal, and they are an important channel for feedback and for correcting exclusion errors in welfare delivery.
sources: Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, Government of India, CPGRAMS portal and About Us. https://pgportal.gov.in/Home/AboutUs
grievance-redressal.example: India's Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) lets a citizen lodge a grievance online against any government organisation, sends it to the ministry, department or state government concerned, and lets the citizen check its status and file an appeal.

participatory-budgeting.definition: A process in which residents directly decide how to allocate part of a public budget, typically at the municipal or local level. Citizens propose, deliberate on, and vote for spending priorities, which are then implemented and monitored. It aims to deepen democratic participation, improve targeting to real local needs, and build trust in government.
sources: Shah, A. (ed.), Participatory Budgeting, World Bank Public Sector Governance and Accountability Series (2007), chapters by Wampler and Goldfrank. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/635011468330986995/pdf/394980REVISED0101OFFICIAL0USE0ONLY1.pdf
participatory-budgeting.example: In Porto Alegre, Brazil, where the model began, residents meet in regional assemblies to set priorities and choose investment projects for part of the city budget.

state-capacity.definition: The ability of a government to carry out its policies across its territory, including raising taxes (fiscal capacity), enforcing contracts, property rights and other rules (legal capacity), and delivering services. These capacities are built through past investments in the state, and legal and fiscal capacity tend to develop together. Weak state capacity means good laws and generous budgets fail to translate into results.
sources: Besley, T. and Persson, T., The Origins of State Capacity: Property Rights, Taxation, and Politics, American Economic Review 99(4) (2009). https://www.lse.ac.uk/economics/Assets/Documents/personal-pages/tim-besley/selected-publications/the-origins-of-state-capacity.pdf

mgnrega.definition: India's Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, which guaranteed at least 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adult members volunteered for unskilled manual work, with an unemployment allowance if work was not provided within 15 days. It worked as a demand-driven safety net and a way of building rural assets. It is being replaced by the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025, which came into force on 1 July 2026, raises the guarantee to 125 days, shares costs between the Centre and states, and repeals MGNREGA from a date the Central Government notifies.
sources: PRS Legislative Research, The VB-G RAM G Bill, 2025 (2025). https://prsindia.org/billtrack/the-viksit-bharat-%E2%80%93-guarantee-for-rozgar-and-ajeevika-mission-gramin-vb-%E2%80%93-g-ram-g-bill-2025
Government of India, The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (Act 36 of 2025), sections 1, 8 and 37. https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/bills_parliament/2025/Viksit_Bharat_G_RAM_G_Act_2025.pdf
India Code, The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, text as on 1 July 2026, footnote to section 1(2) (commencement 1 July 2026, notification S.O. 2382(E) of 11 May 2026). https://www.indiacode.nic.in/
mgnrega.example: A rural household that applied for work under MGNREGA and was not given it within 15 days was entitled to an unemployment allowance from the state government, a provision the 2025 Act retains.

leave-no-one-behind.definition: The central promise of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, by which all UN Member States commit to eradicate poverty in all its forms, end discrimination and exclusion, and reduce the inequalities and vulnerabilities that leave people behind. It means reaching the poorest and also tackling discrimination and its root causes. Making excluded groups visible requires data disaggregated beyond gender, geography and age to all grounds of discrimination, such as disability, caste or ethnicity.
sources: United Nations Sustainable Development Group, Leave No One Behind. https://unsdg.un.org/2030-agenda/universal-values/leave-no-one-behind
leave-no-one-behind.example: A state nutrition programme that breaks down its coverage data by social group and location, and finds that tribal hamlets are being missed, is applying the leave no one behind principle.

rights-holder.definition: A term used in rights-based approaches to describe people as active claimants of entitlements rather than passive beneficiaries or recipients of charity. Framing people as rights-holders shifts attention to the corresponding duty-bearers, usually the state, who are accountable for delivering those rights. The language signals dignity, agency and accountability rather than gratitude.
sources: United Nations Sustainable Development Group, Human Rights-Based Approach. https://unsdg.un.org/2030-agenda/universal-values/human-rights-based-approach
rights-holder.example: A social-audit campaign can treat workers on a public works scheme as rights-holders entitled to their wages and to information about the works, and the state as the duty-bearer accountable for providing them.

sustainable-development-goals.definition: The Sustainable Development Goals are a set of 17 goals and 169 targets adopted by all UN member states in 2015 to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure prosperity by 2030. They succeeded the Millennium Development Goals and apply universally to rich and poor countries alike. Progress is tracked through a global indicator framework and voluntary national reviews.
sources: United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, The 17 Goals. https://sdgs.un.org/goals
sustainable-development-goals.example: India's NITI Aayog publishes an SDG India Index that scores states and union territories on their progress toward the goals.

intergovernmental-panel-on-climate-chang.definition: The IPCC is the United Nations body for assessing the science related to climate change. Created in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme, it provides regular assessments of the scientific basis of climate change, its impacts and future risks, and options for adaptation and mitigation. It does not conduct its own research: volunteer expert authors assess thousands of published studies, and its reports go through open review by experts and governments. Its findings are a key input into international climate negotiations and national policy.
sources: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, About the IPCC. https://www.ipcc.ch/about/
intergovernmental-panel-on-climate-chang.example: A state preparing a climate action plan can draw on the IPCC's assessment of projected heat extremes for its region instead of reviewing the scientific literature from scratch.

climate-adaptation-versus-mitigation.definition: Mitigation is human intervention to reduce greenhouse gas emissions or enhance the sinks that absorb them, which limits the extent of climate change. Adaptation is the process of adjusting to actual or expected climate and its effects, in order to moderate harm or exploit beneficial opportunities. Mitigation addresses the causes of climate change and adaptation its consequences, and most climate strategies need both.
sources: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, AR6 Working Group II, Annex II: Glossary (2022). https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGII_Annex-II.pdf
climate-adaptation-versus-mitigation.example: A coastal district that installs solar mini-grids is mitigating, while building raised flood shelters and promoting saline-tolerant rice is adapting.

just-transition.definition: A set of principles, processes and practices that aim to ensure that no people, workers, places, sectors, countries or regions are left behind in the shift from a high-carbon to a low-carbon economy. It calls for deliberate measures to minimise the negative social and economic effects of the transition and to share its benefits with those most affected, through social dialogue, decent jobs, retraining, social protection, rights at work and economic diversification.
sources: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, AR6 Working Group II, Annex II: Glossary, Just transitions (2022). https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGII_Annex-II.pdf
just-transition.example: A just transition plan for a coal-mining district would pair the phasing out of mines and power plants with retraining for workers, income support and investment in new local industries.

nature-based-solutions.definition: Actions to protect, sustainably manage and restore natural or modified ecosystems that address societal challenges such as climate change, water security and disaster risk effectively and adaptively, while providing benefits for both human well-being and biodiversity. Examples include mangrove restoration, watershed management and urban green spaces.
sources: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, AR6 Working Group II, Annex II: Glossary, Nature-based solution, citing IUCN (2016). https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGII_Annex-II.pdf
nature-based-solutions.example: Restoring mangroves along a cyclone-prone coast can buffer villages against storm surges while supporting fisheries.

loss-and-damage.definition: The harm from climate change impacts and risks, which can be economic, such as destroyed crops and homes, or non-economic, such as loss of life, displacement and cultural heritage. Written with capitals, Loss and Damage refers to the political debate under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, set off by the Warsaw International Mechanism of 2013, about addressing such harm in developing countries that are particularly vulnerable, including through finance from wealthier, high-emitting countries.
sources: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, AR6 Working Group II, Annex II: Glossary, Loss and Damage, and losses and damages (2022). https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGII_Annex-II.pdf
loss-and-damage.example: A small island state whose farmland is permanently lost to sea-level rise, and whose communities have to relocate, suffers loss and damage that adaptation can no longer prevent.

stunting.definition: Stunting is low height-for-age: a child whose height-for-age is more than two standard deviations below the WHO reference median is stunted. It is the result of chronic or recurrent undernutrition, usually associated with poor socioeconomic conditions, poor maternal health and nutrition, frequent illness, and inappropriate infant and young child feeding and care in early life. It holds children back from reaching their physical and cognitive potential, and is a core indicator of a population's early-life deprivation.
sources: World Health Organization, Malnutrition fact sheet. https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malnutrition

International Institute for Population Sciences and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), 2019-21: India Report (2021), chapter 10. https://rchiips.org/nfhs/NFHS-5Reports/NFHS-5_INDIA_REPORT.pdf
stunting.example: India's National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019-21) found that 36 per cent of children under five were stunted.

wasting.definition: Wasting is low weight-for-height. It usually indicates recent and severe weight loss because a child has not had enough to eat or has had an infectious disease, such as diarrhoea, that caused weight loss. Unlike stunting, it reflects acute undernutrition and can develop quickly. A child who is moderately or severely wasted has an increased risk of death, but treatment is possible.
sources: World Health Organization, Malnutrition fact sheet. https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malnutrition

International Institute for Population Sciences and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), 2019-21: India Report (2021), chapter 10. https://rchiips.org/nfhs/NFHS-5Reports/NFHS-5_INDIA_REPORT.pdf
wasting.example: India's National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019-21) found that 19 per cent of children under five were wasted.

multidimensional-poverty-index-2.definition: The Multidimensional Poverty Index measures poverty beyond income by counting the overlapping deprivations a person faces in health, education and living standards, using household survey data. In the global MPI a person deprived in a third or more of ten weighted indicators is counted as poor, and the share of indicators in which they are deprived measures the intensity of their poverty. OPHI computes the global MPI with UNDP's Human Development Report Office, and many governments publish national MPIs to target programmes.
sources: Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative, The global Multidimensional Poverty Index and What is the global MPI? https://ophi.org.uk/what-global-mpi
NITI Aayog, India National Multidimensional Poverty Index: A Progress Review 2023. https://www.niti.gov.in/sites/default/files/2023-08/India-National-Multidimentional-Poverty-Index-2023.pdf
multidimensional-poverty-index-2.example: NITI Aayog's National MPI Progress Review 2023 reported that the share of India's population in multidimensional poverty fell from 24.85 per cent in 2015-16 to 14.96 per cent in 2019-21, about 135 million fewer people.

quality-adjusted-life-year.definition: A QALY measures health outcomes by combining length of life with quality of life: one QALY equals one year of life in perfect health. Each year of life gained from a treatment or intervention is weighted by a quality-of-life score on a scale from 0 to 1, often based on the ability to carry out daily activities and freedom from pain and mental distress. Health technology bodies use the cost per QALY gained to compare the value for money of different interventions.
sources: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), Glossary, Quality-adjusted life year (QALY). https://www.nice.org.uk/glossary?letter=q
quality-adjusted-life-year.example: When evaluating whether to fund a new cataract surgery programme, a state health economist in Tamil Nadu might calculate the cost per QALY gained to compare it against other eye-care options.

participation-ladder.definition: A model devised by Sherry Arnstein in 1969 that ranks public participation on eight rungs according to how much power citizens have over the outcome. The bottom rungs, manipulation and therapy, are non-participation. Informing, consultation and placation are degrees of tokenism, in which people can hear and be heard but cannot make sure their views are acted on. Partnership, delegated power and citizen control are degrees of citizen power. It helps practitioners judge whether people are truly shaping decisions or merely being informed.
sources: Arnstein, S. R., A Ladder of Citizen Participation, Journal of the American Institute of Planners 35(4) (1969). https://doi.org/10.1080/01944366908977225
participation-ladder.example: An urban slum-upgrading project used the participation ladder to see that residents were only being consulted, and redesigned the process to give them decision-making seats.

tokenism.definition: The superficial or symbolic inclusion of members of a marginalised group to give an appearance of fairness or diversity without granting them real influence or addressing underlying inequalities. In participation, it describes involving people for show while decisions are made elsewhere. It is a common failure mode that undermines real participation and representation.
sources: Arnstein, S. R., A Ladder of Citizen Participation, Journal of the American Institute of Planners 35(4) (1969). https://doi.org/10.1080/01944366908977225
tokenism.example: Appointing one woman to a village committee purely to meet a quota, while men set the agenda, is tokenism rather than meaningful participation.

reasonable-accommodation.definition: Necessary and appropriate modifications or adjustments that enable a person with a disability to enjoy rights and participate on an equal basis with others, provided they do not impose a disproportionate burden. Examples include ramps, sign-language interpretation, flexible hours or accessible formats. Denial of reasonable accommodation is itself a form of discrimination under the disability-rights framework.
sources: United Nations, Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Article 2: Definitions. https://www.un.org/development/desa/disabilities/convention-on-the-rights-of-persons-with-disabilities/article-2-definitions.html
reasonable-accommodation.example: A bank that installs a step-free entrance and provides statements in an accessible format for a customer with a visual impairment is offering reasonable accommodation.

construct-validity.definition: The degree to which a measure actually captures the underlying concept, or construct, it claims to measure. It matters whenever a test or scale is interpreted as a measure of an attribute that has no direct operational definition, such as empowerment or self-efficacy, and it is established by building up evidence that scores behave as the theory of the construct predicts.
sources: Cronbach, L. J. and Meehl, P. E., Construct Validity in Psychological Tests, Psychological Bulletin 52 (1955), reproduced in Classics in the History of Psychology, York University. https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Cronbach/construct.htm
construct-validity.example: Whether a five-item scale truly measures 'empowerment' is a question of construct validity.

anonymisation.definition: The process of turning personal data into anonymous information, so that the people it relates to can no longer be identified, directly or indirectly. Techniques include removing direct identifiers, aggregating values and masking. Pseudonymisation, which replaces identifiers with codes that could be linked back, is different, because pseudonymised data can still identify people and remains personal data. Effective anonymisation must guard against re-identification from combinations of indirect variables.
sources: Information Commissioner's Office (UK), Anonymisation guidance: Introduction to anonymisation. https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-sharing/anonymisation/introduction-to-anonymisation/
anonymisation.example: A study on adolescent health in Delhi anonymised transcripts by replacing names and school details with codes before sharing them with external analysts.

digital-personal-data-protection-act.definition: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which governs the processing of digital personal data. It places duties on data fiduciaries, gives rights to individuals, called data principals, and sets requirements on notice and consent, purpose limitation and security, with special protections for children's data, meaning anyone under eighteen. It is enforced by a Data Protection Board of India. Under the notification of 13 November 2025, the provisions on the Board came into force on publication, and the main duties, rights and penalties come into force eighteen months later, in May 2027. Development organisations handling beneficiary data in India must align their practices with it by then.
sources: Government of India, The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023), Gazette of India Extraordinary, 11 August 2023 (CG-DL-E-12082023-248045). https://egazette.gov.in/

Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Notification G.S.R. 843(E) of 13 November 2025 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Gazette of India (CG-DL-E-14112025-267647). https://egazette.gov.in/
digital-personal-data-protection-act.example: An NGO running a digital cash-transfer platform reviewed its consent forms and data-retention rules to comply with the DPDP Act before onboarding new users.

inclusion-error.definition: A targeting mistake where ineligible people are wrongly included as beneficiaries (leakage).
sources: Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Economic Survey 2016-17, Chapter 9: Universal Basic Income (2017). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/budget2017-2018/es2016-17/echap09.pdf
inclusion-error.example: An inclusion error meant better-off families received the subsidy meant for the poor.

care-economy.definition: The paid and unpaid work involved in caring for people. Care work covers direct, personal care, such as feeding a baby or nursing a sick relative, and indirect care, such as cooking and cleaning. Much of it is unpaid, is done mostly by women and girls, and is left out of conventional measures of economic output such as GDP. The ILO frames the policy agenda as recognising, reducing and redistributing unpaid care work, alongside more and decent paid care jobs.
sources: International Labour Organization, Care work and care jobs for the future of decent work (2018). https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/@dgreports/@dcomm/@publ/documents/publication/wcms_633135.pdf
Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Government of India, Time Use in India 2024. https://www.mospi.gov.in/
care-economy.example: India's Time Use Survey 2024 found that, averaged over everyone aged six and above, women spent 236 minutes a day on unpaid domestic services for their households and 47 minutes on unpaid caregiving, against 24 and 13 minutes for men.

feminisation-of-poverty.definition: The pattern in which women and female-headed households bear a disproportionate share of poverty, linked to wage gaps, unpaid care burdens, insecure land and asset rights and limited social protection. The concept highlights that poverty is gendered in both its causes and its lived experience; the Beijing Platform for Action called for research to address it. Critics caution against over-simplifying it, since female-headed households are diverse and not uniformly poorer.
sources: United Nations, Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (1995), Critical area A: Women and Poverty. https://www.un.org/womenwatch/daw/beijing/platform/poverty.htm
feminisation-of-poverty.example: A widow who loses access to her late husband's land under local custom can fall into deeper poverty than a man in the same household would have, which is the kind of gendered vulnerability the concept points to.

gender-pay-gap.definition: The average difference in earnings between women and men across a workforce, usually expressed as a percentage of men's pay. It reflects a mix of factors including occupational segregation, undervaluation of feminised work, career interruptions for care, and outright discrimination. The unadjusted gap compares all workers, while the adjusted gap controls for role, hours and experience.
sources: International Labour Organization, Global Wage Report 2018/19: What lies behind gender pay gaps (2018). https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/@dgreports/@dcomm/@publ/documents/publication/wcms_650553.pdf
gender-pay-gap.example: The ILO's Global Wage Report 2018/19, covering some 70 countries, found that women are paid on average about 20 per cent less than men, and that much of the gap cannot be explained by differences in education, experience or other labour market characteristics.

gender-based-violence.definition: Harmful acts directed at a person because of their gender or gender norms, including physical, sexual, psychological and economic violence, whether in the home, workplace or public space. It is rooted in unequal power relations and disproportionately affects women, girls and gender-diverse people. Programmes address it through prevention, survivor-centred response services, and legal reform.
sources: World Health Organization, Violence against women fact sheet, citing the UN Declaration on the Elimination of Violence against Women. https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/violence-against-women
gender-based-violence.example: A health facility that trains staff to identify intimate partner violence, offers confidential care and refers survivors to legal and counselling services is providing a survivor-centred response to gender-based violence.

safeguarding.definition: The organisational responsibility to take all reasonable steps to protect people, especially children and vulnerable adults, from harm, abuse, exploitation and neglect caused by staff, programmes or partners. It covers preventing harm, listening to people at risk, responding sensitively and robustly to allegations, and learning from every case, through safe recruitment, codes of conduct, confidential reporting channels and survivor-centred response. In the aid sector it is often framed as protection from sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment (SEAH).
sources: Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (UK), Safeguarding and protection from sexual exploitation and abuse and harassment (SEAH) in international work. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/safeguarding-against-sexual-exploitation-and-abuse-and-sexual-harassment-seah-in-the-aid-sector
safeguarding.example: After signing a donor agreement, an Indian NGO introduced a safeguarding policy with a whistle-blower hotline and mandatory background checks for field staff working with children.

social-exclusion.definition: A state in which individuals or groups are unable to participate fully in economic, social, political and cultural life, and the process that leads to and sustains it. It often runs along lines of caste, ethnicity, gender, religion, disability or poverty, and involves lack of access to resources and services as well as lack of voice and of equal respect for rights. It is multidimensional, so it goes beyond low income. The counterpart goal is social inclusion.
sources: United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Report on the World Social Situation 2016: Leaving No One Behind: The Imperative of Inclusive Development, chapter 1. https://www.un.org/esa/socdev/rwss/2016/full-report.pdf
social-exclusion.example: A community barred by caste norms from shared water sources, temples and public spaces faces social exclusion that a rise in its income alone would not remove.

disability-inclusion.definition: The practice of ensuring persons with disabilities can participate fully and equally in all aspects of development. It follows the understanding in the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities that disability arises when long-term physical, mental, intellectual or sensory impairments interact with barriers that hinder full participation on an equal basis with others, so the task is to remove those barriers. It spans accessible infrastructure and information, inclusive services, reasonable accommodation, representation in decision-making and disaggregated data.
sources: United Nations, Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Article 1 and Article 2. https://www.un.org/development/desa/disabilities/convention-on-the-rights-of-persons-with-disabilities/article-1-purpose.html
disability-inclusion.example: A district education office that makes school buildings step-free, provides textbooks in accessible formats and records disability in its enrolment data is practising disability inclusion.

data-ethics.definition: The principles governing the responsible collection, storage, sharing and use of data about people. Government frameworks such as the UK's rest on transparency, accountability and fairness, and in practice data ethics also covers consent, privacy, security and avoiding harm. In development it addresses the power imbalance between those who collect data and the communities it describes. It goes beyond, and sits alongside, compliance with data-protection law and research-ethics standards.
sources: Government Digital Service (UK), Data and AI Ethics Framework (2020, updated 2025). https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/data-ethics-framework
data-ethics.example: Before mapping households for a poverty survey, an organisation adopted a data-ethics protocol limiting who could see GPS coordinates that might expose vulnerable families.

learning-poverty.definition: Learning poverty is the share of ten-year-olds who cannot read and understand a simple age-appropriate text. Coined by the World Bank and UNESCO, it combines out-of-school children with those in school who are not learning to read. It reframes education success around actual learning rather than mere enrolment or attendance.
sources: World Bank, Ending Learning Poverty: What Will It Take? (2019). https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/395151571251399043/pdf/Ending-Learning-Poverty-What-Will-It-Take.pdf
learning-poverty.example: When the World Bank introduced the measure in 2019, it estimated that 53 per cent of children in low- and middle-income countries were in learning poverty.

foundational-literacy-and-numeracy.definition: FLN refers to the basic reading, writing, and arithmetic skills children should master in the early primary grades before moving to more complex learning. Weak foundations compound over time, leaving children unable to follow later curricula. It has become a central policy priority because so many students progress through grades without these basics.
sources: Ministry of Human Resource Development, Government of India, National Education Policy 2020, chapter 2. https://www.education.gov.in/sites/upload_files/mhrd/files/NEP_Final_English_0.pdf
foundational-literacy-and-numeracy.example: India's National Education Policy 2020 set the goal that every student attain foundational literacy and numeracy by Grade 3 and called for a National Mission on Foundational Literacy and Numeracy.

teacher-absenteeism.definition: Teacher absenteeism is the rate at which teachers are absent from their assigned schools during working hours, whether on unauthorised leave or diverted to other duties. High rates waste public spending, reduce instructional time, and are a persistent constraint on learning in low-income settings. It is typically measured through unannounced school visits.
sources: Muralidharan, K., Das, J., Holla, A. and Mohpal, A., The Fiscal Cost of Weak Governance: Evidence from Teacher Absence in India, NBER Working Paper 20299 (2014). https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w20299/w20299.pdf
teacher-absenteeism.example: A nationally representative study of over 3,000 government primary schools in 19 Indian states found that over 25 per cent of teachers were absent on a typical working day in 2003, and a 2010 resurvey of rural India still found 23.6 per cent absent during unannounced visits.

graduation-approach.definition: A sequenced, time-bound package designed to move households in extreme poverty onto sustainable livelihoods. It combines a one-time transfer of a productive asset, training to manage it, consumption support for a few months to a year, access to savings, and frequent coaching home visits, and often a health component. It was developed by BRAC in Bangladesh in 2002 as Targeting the Ultra Poor. Randomised evaluations in several countries found large and long-lasting gains in households' standard of living.
sources: J-PAL, Building stable livelihoods for low-income households (Policy Insight). https://www.povertyactionlab.org/policy-insight/building-stable-livelihoods-ultra-poor
graduation-approach.example: Under BRAC's programme, a woman might receive cows or goats, training in looking after them, a small regular cash or food allowance for some months, and regular visits from a coach.

self-help-group.definition: A small, self-managed community group, in India mostly of women from poor rural households, that gives members access to finance, including bank credit, and serves as a platform for livelihood, social and entitlement work. Under the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM), SHGs are federated into larger community institutions.
sources: Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Economic Survey 2025-26, Chapter 13: Rural Development and Social Progress, paragraphs 13.46 to 13.48 and Table XIII.1. https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/economicsurvey/doc/eschapter/echap13.pdf
self-help-group.example: By December 2025, DAY-NRLM had promoted about 90.9 lakh SHGs, mobilising about 10 crore rural households.

proxy-means-test-2.definition: A targeting method that estimates household welfare from observable assets and characteristics when income is hard to measure.
sources: Mansuri, G. and Rao, V., Localizing Development: Does Participation Work?, World Bank Policy Research Report (2013), chapter 5 notes 2 and 7. https://doi.org/10.1596/978-0-8213-8256-1
proxy-means-test-2.example: The state used a proxy means test to identify eligible households for the housing subsidy.

policy-coherence.definition: The extent to which different policies and government actions reinforce rather than undermine one another in pursuit of shared objectives. Incoherence arises when one ministry's incentives cancel out another's goals, or when domestic policies contradict development commitments. Achieving coherence requires coordination mechanisms, whole-of-government planning, and attention to trade-offs.
sources: OECD, Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development, second edition (2023), Coherence and Policy coherence for sustainable development. https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2023/06/glossary-of-key-terms-in-evaluation-and-results-based-management-for-sustainable-development-second-edition_2767e14e/632da462-en-fr-es.pdf
policy-coherence.example: A country promoting clean air while simultaneously subsidising diesel and coal shows policy incoherence, as fiscal policy pulls against environmental policy.

cash-transfer.definition: A social protection tool that provides money directly to poor households, either unconditionally or conditional on behaviours such as children's school attendance or health check-ups. Transfers aim to raise consumption, reduce poverty and let recipients choose their own priorities, and conditional transfers also aim to encourage investment in children's education and health.
sources: Gertler, P. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, World Bank (2011), Box 1.1: The Progresa/Oportunidades Conditional Cash Transfer Program in Mexico. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/823791468325239704/pdf/Impact-evaluation-in-practice.pdf
Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Economic Survey 2016-17, Chapter 9: Universal Basic Income (2017). https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/budget2017-2018/es2016-17/echap09.pdf
cash-transfer.example: Mexico's Progresa programme, launched in the 1990s, paid cash to mothers in poor households on condition that their children attended school regularly and visited a health centre.

evidence-based-policy.definition: An approach to policymaking that systematically uses evidence, including monitoring data, evaluations and research, to inform decisions rather than relying on ideology, anecdote or precedent alone. It shifts attention from inputs to outcomes and results, and asks what works, for whom and at what cost. Evidence is one input alongside political, ethical and contextual considerations, which is why many practitioners prefer the term evidence-informed policy.
sources: Gertler, P. et al., Impact Evaluation in Practice, World Bank (2011), chapter 1, Evidence-Based Policy Making and Box 1.1. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/823791468325239704/pdf/Impact-evaluation-in-practice.pdf
evidence-based-policy.example: In Mexico, impact evaluation results from the Progresa conditional cash transfer programme supported the new government's decision in 2001 to continue and expand it.
